sections.title: Appendix B Detailed Discussion of Related Work
path: Appendix B Detailed Discussion of Related Work

paragraphs.text: In this section, we discuss related work in greater detail, including relevant works not already covered.
Self-improvement and self-training

Our work is most directly related to a growing body of empirical research that studies self-improvement/self-training for language models in a supervision-free setting in which there is no external feedback (Huang et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022b; Pang et al., 2023), and takes a first step toward providing a theoretical understanding for these methods. There is also a closely related body of research on “LLM-as-a-Judge” techniques, which investigates approaches to designing self-reward functions $r_{\texttt{self}}$, often based on specific prompting techniques (Zheng et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024a; Wang et al., 2024).

A somewhat complementary line of research develops algorithms based on self-training and self-play (Zelikman et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024c; Qu et al., 2024), but leverages various forms of external feedback (e.g., positive examples for SFT or explicit reward signal). These methods typically outperform feedback-free self-improvement methods (Zelikman et al., 2022). However, in many scenarios, obtaining external feedback can be costly or laborious; it may require collecting high-quality labeled/annotated data, rewriting examples in a formal language, etc. Thus, these two approaches are not directly comparable.

We also mention that the self-improvement problem we study is related to a classical line of research on self-distillation (Buciluǎ et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015; Devlin, 2018; Pham et al., 2021; Rizve et al., 2021), but this specific form of self-training has received limited investigation in the context of language modeling.
Entropy minimization

Sharpening is also closely related to a line of work on entropy minimization or minimum entropy regularization, where we seek models that have high predictive accuracy and low entropy/uncertainty. This line of work originated in the semi-supervised learning literature (Grandvalet and Bengio, 2004) and was popularized as a test-time adaptation method in computer vision (Wang et al., 2020; Press et al., 2024, c.f.,). Maximum-likelihood sharpening, especially via RL, is closely related in that Equation 5 with $\beta\to 0$ and $r_{\texttt{self}}=\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}$ maximizes $\En_{\pi}[\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x)]$ rather than $-H(\pi)=\En_{\pi}[\log\pi(y\mid{}x)]$. (It is important that the latter is optimized continuously with $\pi_{\texttt{base}}$ as an initialization, but when this is done it can be seen to sharpen $\pi_{\texttt{base}}$, at least heuristically.) Prior work in this direction is largely empirical, focused on computer vision domains with small output spaces $\mathcal{Y}$, and hence studies statistical benefits of entropy minimization. In contrast, we initiate a theoretical study of sharpening, are primarily motivated by applications to language modeling with exponentially large output spaces, and view sharpening primarily as a computational phenomena. However, it would be interesting to understand whether statistical benefits observed in computer vision translate to the language modeling setting.
Alignment and RLHF

The specific algorithms for self-improvement/sharpening we study can be viewed as special cases of standard alignment algorithms, including classical RLHF methods (Christiano et al., 2017; Bai et al., 2022a; Ouyang et al., 2022), direct alignment (Rafailov et al., 2023), and (inference-time or training-time) best-of-$N$ methods (Amini et al., 2024; Sessa et al., 2024; Gui et al., 2024; Pace et al., 2024). However, the maximum likelihood sharpening objective (3) used for our theoretical results has been relatively unexplored within the alignment literature.
Inference-time decoding

Many inference-time decoding strategies such as greedy/low-temperature decoding, beam-search (Meister et al., 2020), and chain-of-thought decoding (Wang and Zhou, 2024) can be viewed as instances of inference-time sharpening for specific choices of the self-reward function $r_{\texttt{self}}$. More sophisticated inference-time search strategies such tree search and MCTS (Yao et al., 2024; Wan et al., 2024; Mudgal et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024) are also related, though this line of work frequently makes use of external reward signals or verification, which is somewhat complementary to our work.
Theoretical guarantees for self-training

On the theoretical side, current understanding of self-training is limited. One line of work, focusing on the self-distillation objective (Hinton et al., 2015) for binary classification and regression, aims to provide convergence guarantees for self-training in stylized setups such as linear models (Mobahi et al., 2020; Das and Sanghavi, 2023; Das et al., 2024; Pareek et al., 2024), with Allen-Zhu and Li (2020) giving guarantees for feedforward neural networks. Perhaps most closely related to our work is Frei et al. (2022), who show that self-training on a model’s pseudo-labels can amplify the margin for linear logistic regression. However, to the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to study self-training in a general framework that subsumes language modeling.

Our results for RLHF-Sharpening are related to a body of work that provides sample complexity guarantees for alignment methods (Zhu et al., 2023; Xiong et al., 2023; Ye et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Song et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024), but our results leverage the structure of the maximum-likelihood sharpening self-reward function $r_{\texttt{self}}(y\mid{}x)=\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x)$, and provide guarantees for the sharpening objective in Section 3.1 instead of the usual notion of reward suboptimality used in reinforcement learning theory.

Lastly, we mention that our results—particularly our amortization perspective on self-improvement—are related to work that studies representational advantages afforded by additional inference time (Malach, 2023; Li et al., 2024). These work focus on truly sequential tasks, while our work focuses on the complementary question of amortizing parallel computation. Thus the representational implications are quite different.
Optimization versus sampling

The maximum-likelihood sharpening objective we introduce in Section 3 connects the study of self-improvement to a large body of research in theoretical computer science on computational tradeoffs (e.g., separations and equivalences) between optimization and sampling (Barahona, 1982; Kirkpatrick et al., 1983; Lovász and Vempala, 2006; Singh and Vishnoi, 2014; Ma et al., 2019; Talwar, 2019; Eldan et al., 2022). On the one hand, this line of research highlights that there exist natural classes of distributions for which sampling is tractable, yet maximum likelihood optimization is intractable, and vice-versa. On the other hand, various works in this line of research also demonstrate computational reductions between optimization and sampling, whereby optimization can be reduced to sampling and vice-versa.

Our setting indeed includes natural model classes where one should not expect there to be a computational reduction from optimization ($\argmax_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x)$) to sampling ($y\sim\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\cdot\mid{}x)$), and hence inference-time sharpening is computationally intractable (Section E.1). Of course, coverage assumptions eliminate this intractability. For training-time sharpening (where the goal is to amortize across prompts by training a sharpened model, as formulated in Section 3) the obstacle in natural, concrete model classes is not just computational but in fact representational (Section E.2). Regarding the latter point, we note that while amortized Bayesian inference has received extensive investigation empirically (Beal, 2003; Gershman and Goodman, 2014; Swersky et al., 2020; Bengio et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2023), we are unaware of theoretical guarantees outside of this work.

sections.title: Appendix C Guarantees for Inference-Time Sharpening
path: Appendix C Guarantees for Inference-Time Sharpening

paragraphs.text: In this section, we give theoretical guarantees for the inference-time best-of-$N$ sampling algorithm for sharpening described in Section 3.1, under the maximum-likelihood sharpening self-reward function
r_{\texttt{self}}(y\mid{}x;\pi_{\texttt{base}})=\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x).

Recall that given a prompt $x\in\mathcal{X}$, the inference-time best-of-$N$ sampling algorithm draws $N$ responses $y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}\sim\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\cdot\mid{}x)$, then return the response $\widehat{y}=\argmax_{y_{i}}\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y_{i}\mid{}x)$. We show that this algorithm returns an approximate maximizer for the maximum-likelihood sharpening objective whenever the base policy $\pi_{\texttt{base}}$ has sufficient coverage. For a parameter $\gamma\in[0,1)$ we define
\displaystyle\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\vcentcolon={}\left\{y\mid{}\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x)\geq{}(1-\gamma)\cdot\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid x)\right\}
as the set of $(1-\gamma)$-approximate maximizers for $\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x)$ (see Section F.1 for background on $\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)$).
Let a prompt $x\in\mathcal{X}$ be given. For any $\rho\in(0,1)$ and $\gamma\in[0,1)$, as long as
\displaystyle N\geq\frac{\log(\rho^{-1})}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)},

Proof of Appendix C. Fix a prompt $x\in\mathcal{X}$, failure probability $\rho\in(0,1)$, and parameter $\gamma\in(0,1)$. paragraphs.text: SFT-Sharpening is a simple and natural self-training scheme, and converges to a sharpened policy as $n,N\to\infty$. However, using a fixed response sample size $N$ may be wasteful for prompts where the model is confident. To this end, in this section we introduce and analyze, a variant of SFT-Sharpening based on adaptive sampling, which adjusts the number of sampled responses adaptively.
Algorithm

We present the adaptive SFT-Sharpening algorithm only for the special case of the maximum likelihood sharpening self-reward. Let a stopping parameter $\mu>0$ be given. For $x_{i}\in\mathcal{X}$, and $y_{i,1},y_{i,2}\ldots\sim\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\cdot\mid{}x_{i})$, define a stopping time (e.g., Benjamini and Hochberg (1995)) via:
\displaystyle N_{\mu}(x_{i}):=\inf\left\{k:\frac{1}{\max_{1\leq j\leq k}\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y_{i,j}\mid{}x_{i})}\leq\frac{k}{\mu}\right\}.
The adaptive SFT-Sharpening algorithm computes adaptively sampled responses $y^{\texttt{AdaBoN}}_{i}$ via
y^{\texttt{AdaBoN}}_{i}\sim\argmax\left\{\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y_{i,j}\mid{}x_{i})\mid{}y_{i,1},\ldots,y_{i,N_{\mu}(x_{i})}\right\},
then trains the sharpened model through SFT:
\widehat{\pi}^{\texttt{AdaBoN}}=\argmax_{\pi\in\Pi}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\pi(y^{\texttt{AdaBoN}}_{i}\mid{}x_{i}).
Critically, by using scheme in Eq. 32, this algorithm can stop sampling responses for the prompt $x_{i}$ if it becomes clear that the confidence is large.
Theoretical guarantee
We now show that adaptive SFT-Sharpening enjoys provable benefits over its non-adaptive counterpart through the dependence on the accuracy parameter $\epsilon>0$.

Given $x\in\mathcal{X}$, and $y_{1},y_{2}\ldots\sim\pi_{\texttt{base}}(x)$, let $N_{\mu}(x):=\inf big\{k:\frac{1}{\max_{1\leq i\leq k}\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y_{i}\mid{}x)}\leq k/\mu big\}$, and define a random variable $y^{\texttt{AdaBoN}}(x)\sim\argmax\left\{\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y_{i}\mid{}x)\mid{}y_{1},\ldots,y_{N_{\mu}}\sim\pi_{\texttt{base}}(x)\right\}$. Let $\pi^{\texttt{AdaBoN}}_{\mu}(x)$ denote the distribution over $y^{\texttt{AdaBoN}}(x)$. We make the following realizability assumption. The model class $\Pi$ satisfies $\pi^{\texttt{AdaBoN}}_{\mu}\in\Pi$. Compared to SFT-Sharpening, we require a somewhat stronger coverage coefficient given by
\displaystyle\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{C}_{\texttt{cov}}=\En_{x\sim\mu}\left[\frac{1}{\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x)}\right].
This definition coincides with Eq. 14 when the arg-max response is unique, but is larger in general.

Our main theoretical guarantee for adaptive SFT-Sharpening is as follows. Let $\delta,\rho\in(0,1)$ be given. Set $\mu=\ln(2\delta^{-1})$, and assume Appendix D holds. Then with probability at least $1-\rho$, the adaptive SFT-Sharpening algorithm has
\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}[\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\star}(x)\mid x)\leq 1-\delta]\lesssim\frac{\log(|\Pi|\rho^{-1})}{\delta n},

and has sample complexity $\En[m]=n\cdot\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{C}_{\texttt{cov}}\log(\delta^{-1})$. Taking $n\gtrsim\frac{\log(|\Pi|\rho^{-1})}{\delta\epsilon}$ ensures that with probability at least $1-\rho$, $\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}[\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\star}(x)\mid x)\leq 1-\delta]\leq\epsilon$, and gives total sample complexity
\displaystyle\En\left[m\right]=O\left(\frac{\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{C}_{\texttt{cov}}\log(\lvert\Pi\rvert\rho^{-1})\log(\delta^{-1})}{\delta\epsilon}\right).

Compared to the result for SFT-Sharpening in Section 4.1, this shows that adaptive SFT-Sharpening achieves sample complexity scaling with $\frac{1}{\epsilon}$ instead of $\frac{1}{\epsilon^{2}}$. We believe the dependence on $\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{C}_{\texttt{cov}}$ for this algorithm is tight, as the adaptive stopping rule used in the algorithm can be overly conservative when $\lvert\bm{y}^{\star}(x)\rvert$ is large.
A matching lower bound

We now prove a complementary lower bound, which shows that the $\epsilon$-dependence in Appendix D is tight. To do so, we consider the following adaptive variant of the sample-and-evaluate framework. [Adaptive sample-and-evaluate framework] In the Adaptive Sample-and-Evaluate framework, the learner is allowed to sample $n$ prompts $x\sim\mu$, and sample an arbitrary, adaptively chosen number of samples $y_{1},y_{2},\dots\sim\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\cdot\mid x)$ before sampling a new prompt $x^{\prime}\sim\mu$. In this framework we define sample complexity $m$ as the total number of pairs $(x,y)$ sampled by the algorithm, which is a random variable. Our main lower bound is as follows. [Lower bound for sharpening under adaptive sampling] Fix an integer $d\geq 1$ and parameters $\epsilon\in(0,1)$ and $C\geq 1$. There exists a class of models $\Pi$ such that (i) $\log|\Pi|\eqsim d(1+\log(C\epsilon^{-1}))$, (ii) $\sup_{\pi\in\Pi}C_{\texttt{cov}}(\pi)\lesssim C$, and (iii) $\bm{y}^{\pi}(x)$ is a singleton for all $\pi\in\Pi$, for which any sharpening algorithm $\widehat{\pi}$ in the adaptive sample-and-evaluate framework that achieves $\En\left[\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}[\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\pi_{\texttt{base}}}(x)\mid{}x)>1/2]\right]\geq 1-\epsilon$ for all $\pi_{\texttt{base}}\in\Pi$ must collect a total number of samples $m=n\cdot{}N$ at least
\displaystyle\En[m]\gtrsim\frac{C\log|\Pi|}{\epsilon\cdot{}(1+\log(C\epsilon^{-1}))}.
Appendix D is a special case of a more general theorem, Appendix H, which is stated and proven in Appendix H.

sections.title: Appendix E Computational and Representational Challenges in Sharpening
path: Appendix E Computational and Representational Challenges in Sharpening

paragraphs.text: In this section, we make several basic observations about the inherent computational and representational challenges of maximum-likelihood sharpening. First, in Section E.1, we focus on computational challenges, and show that computing a sharpened response for a given prompt $x$ can be computationally intractable in general, even when sampling $y\sim\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\cdot\mid{}x)$ can be performed efficiently. Then, in Section E.2, we shift our focus to representational challenges, and show that even if $\pi_{\texttt{base}}$ is an autoregressive model, the “sharpened” version of $\pi_{\texttt{base}}$ may not be representable as an autoregressive model with the same architecture. These results motivate the statistical assumptions (coverage and realizability) made in our analysis of SFT-Sharpening and RLHF-Sharpening in Section 4.

To make the results in this section precise, we work in perhaps the simplest special case of autoregressive language modelling, where the model class consists of multi-layer linear softmax models. Formally, let $\mathcal{X}$ be the space of prompts, and let $\mathcal{Y}:=\mathcal{V}^{H}$ be the space of responses, where $\mathcal{V}$ is the vocabulary space and $H$ is the horizon. For a collection of fixed/known $d$-dimensional feature mappings $\phi_{h}:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{V}^{h}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and a norm parameter $B$, we define the model class $\Pi_{\phi,B,H}$ as the set of models
\displaystyle\pi_{\theta}(y_{1:H}\mid{}x)=\prod_{h=1}^{H}\pi_{\theta_{h}}(y_{h}\mid{}x,y_{1:h-1})
where
\pi_{\theta}(y_{h}\mid{}x,y_{1:h-1})\propto\exp(\langle\phi(x,y_{1:h}),\theta_{h}\rangle)
and $\theta=(\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{H})\in(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{H}$ is any tuple with $\lVert\theta_{h}\rVert_{2}\leq B$ for all $h\in[H]$.

sections.title: E.1 Computational Challenges
path: Appendix E Computational and Representational Challenges in Sharpening

paragraphs.text: Given query access to $\phi$, for any given parameter vector $\theta$ and prompt $x$, sampling from a linear softmax model $\pi_{\theta}$ (Eq. 39) is computationally tractable, since it only requires time $\mathrm{poly}(H,|\mathcal{V}|,d)$. Similarly, evaluating $\pi_{\theta}(y_{1:H}\mid{}x)$ for given prompt $x$ and response $y_{1:H}$ is computationally tractable. However, the following proposition shows that computing the sharpened response $\argmax_{y_{1:H}\in\mathcal{V}^{H}}\pi_{\theta}(y_{1:H}\mid{}x)$ for a given parameter $\theta$ and response $x$ is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard. Hence, even inference-time sharpening is computationally intractable in the worst case.

Set $\mathcal{X}=\{\perp\}$ and $\mathcal{V}=\{-1,1\}$. Set $d=d(H):=H+H^{2}+H^{3}$. Identifying $[d]$ with $[H]\sqcup[H]^{2}\sqcup[H]^{3}$, we define $\phi_{h}:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{V}^{h}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}$ by $\phi_{h}(\perp,y_{1:h})_{i}=y_{i}$ and $\phi_{h}(\perp,y_{1:h})_{(i,j)}=y_{i}y_{j}$ and $\phi_{h}(\perp,y_{1:h})_{(i,j,k)}=y_{i}y_{j}y_{k}$. There is a function $B(H)\leq\mathrm{poly}(H)$ such that the following problem is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard: given $\theta=(\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{H})$ with $\max_{h\in[H]}\lVert\theta_{h}\rVert_{2}\leq B(H)$, compute any element of $\argmax_{y_{1:H}\in\mathcal{V}^{H}}\pi_{\theta}(y_{1:H}\mid{}x)$. Note that our results in Section 4 and Appendix C bypass this hardness through the assumption that the coverage parameter $C_{\texttt{cov}}$ is bounded.

Proof of Section E.1. Fix $H$ and recall that $d(H)=H+H^{2}+H^{3}$. We define three collection of basis vectors: $\left\{e_{h}\right\}_{h\in[H]}$ cover the first $H$ coordinates, $\left\{e_{(h,h^{\prime})}\right\}_{h,h^{\prime}\in[H]^{2}}$ cover the next $H^{2}$ coordinates, and $\left\{e_{(h,h^{\prime},h^{\prime\prime})}\right\}_{h,h^{\prime},h^{\prime\prime}\in[H]^{3}}$ cover the last $H^{3}$ coordinates. Suppose we define $\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{H-2}=0$, so that $\pi_{\theta}(y_{h}|x,y_{1:h-1})=1/2$ for all $1\leq h\leq H-2$. Define $\theta_{H-1}=\sum_{1\leq i,j\leq H-2}J_{ij}e_{(i,j,H-1)}$ for a matrix $J\in\mathbb{R}^{(H-2)\times(H-2)}$ to be specified later, and define $\theta_{H}=\frac{B}{2}(e_{(H-1,H)}+e_{H})$. Then $2^{H-2}\cdot\pi_{\theta}(y_{1:H}\mid{}\perp)\leq 1/2$ for any $y_{1:H}$ with $y_{H-1}=-1$ or $y_{H}=-1$, since this implies that $\pi_{\theta_{H}}(y_{H}\mid{}\perp,y_{1:H-1})\leq{}1/2$. Meanwhile, for any $y_{1:H}$ with $y_{H-1}=y_{H}=1$, we have

2^{H-2}\cdot\pi_{\theta}(y_{1:H}\mid{}\perp)=\frac{\exp\left(\sum_{i,j\leq{}H-2}J_{ij}y_{i}y_{j}\right)}{\exp\left(\sum_{i,j\leq{}H-2}J_{ij}y_{i}y_{j}\right)+\exp\left(-\sum_{i,j\leq{}H-2}J_{ij}y_{i}y_{j}\right)}\cdot\frac{\exp(B)}{\exp(B)+\exp(-B)}.

Let $G$ be any graph on vertex set $[H-2]$ and let $J=-A(G)$ where $A(G)$ is the adjacency matrix of $G$. Then among $y_{1:H}$ with $y_{H-1}=y_{H}=1$, $2^{H-2}\cdot\pi_{\theta}(y_{1:H}\mid{}\perp)$ is maximized when $y_{1:H-2}$ corresponds to a max-cut in $G$. If $G$ has an odd number of edges, then some max-cut removes strictly more than half of the edges, and for the corresponding sequence $y_{1:H}$ we have $2^{H-2}\cdot\pi_{\theta}(y_{1:H}\mid{}\perp)\geq(1/2+\Omega(1))\cdot(1-\exp(-\Omega(B)))$, which is greater than $1/2$ when we take $B:=H$ and $H$ is sufficiently large. Thus, computing $\argmax_{y_{1:H}\in\mathcal{V}^{H}}\pi_{\theta}(y_{1:H}\mid{}\perp)$ yields a max-cut of $G$. It is well-known that computing a max-cut in a graph is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard, and the assumption that $G$ has an odd number of edges is without loss of generality. ∎

Set $\mathcal{X}=\{\perp\}$ and $\mathcal{V}=\{-1,1\}$. Set $d=d(H):=H+H^{2}+H^{3}$. There is a function $B(H)\leq\mathrm{poly}(H)$ such that the following problem is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard: given $\theta=(\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{H})$ with $\max_{h\in[H]}\lVert\theta_{h}\rVert_{2}\leq B(H)$, compute any element of $\argmax_{y_{1:H}\in\mathcal{V}^{H}}\pi_{\theta}(y_{1:H}\mid{}x)$. Note that our results in Section 4 and Appendix C bypass this hardness through the assumption that the coverage parameter $C_{\texttt{cov}}$ is bounded.

Proof of Section E.1. Fix $H$ and recall that $d(H)=H+H^{2}+H^{3}$. We define three collection of basis vectors: $\left\{e_{h}\right\}_{h\in[H]}$ cover the first $H$ coordinates, $\left\{e_{(h,h^{\prime})}\right\}_{h,h^{\prime}\in[H]^{2}}$ cover the next $H^{2}$ coordinates, and $\left\{e_{(h,h^{\prime},h^{\prime\prime})}\right\}_{h,h^{\prime},h^{\prime\prime}\in[H]^{3}}$ cover the last $H^{3}$ coordinates. Suppose we define $\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{H-2}=0$, so that $\pi_{\theta}(y_{h}|x,y_{1:h-1})=1/2$ for all $1\leq h\leq H-2$. Define $\theta_{H-1}=\sum_{1\leq i,j\leq H-2}J_{ij}e_{(i,j,H-1)}$ for a matrix $J\in\mathbb{R}^{(H-2)\times(H-2)}$ to be specified later, and define $\theta_{H}=\frac{B}{2}(e_{(H-1,H)}+e_{H})$. Then $2^{H-2}\cdot\pi_{\theta}(y_{1:H}\mid{}\perp)\leq 1/2$ for any $y_{1:H}$ with $y_{H-1}=-1$ or $y_{H}=-1$, since this implies that $\pi_{\theta_{H}}(y_{H}\mid{}\perp,y_{1:H-1})\leq{}1/2$. Meanwhile, for any $y_{1:H}$ with $y_{H-1}=y_{H}=1$, we have

2^{H-2}\cdot\pi_{\theta}(y_{1:H}\mid{}\perp)=\frac{\exp\left(\sum_{i,j\leq{}H-2}J_{ij}y_{i}y_{j}\right)}{\exp\left(\sum_{i,j\leq{}H-2}J_{ij}y_{i}y_{j}\right)+\exp\left(-\sum_{i,j\leq{}H-2}J_{ij}y_{i}y_{j}\right)}\cdot\frac{\exp(B)}{\exp(B)+\exp(-B)}.

Let $G$ be any graph on vertex set $[H-2]$ and let $J=-A(G)$ where $A(G)$ is the adjacency matrix of $G$. Then among $y_{1:H}$ with $y_{H-1}=y_{H}=1$, $2^{H-2}\cdot\pi_{\theta}(y_{1:H}\mid{}\perp)$ is maximized when $y_{1:H-2}$ corresponds to a max-cut in $G$. If $G$ has an odd number of edges, then some max-cut removes strictly more than half of the edges, and for the corresponding sequence $y_{1:H}$ we have $2^{H-2}\cdot\pi_{\theta}(y_{1:H}\mid{}\perp)\geq(1/2+\Omega(1))\cdot(1-\exp(-\Omega(B)))$, which is greater than $1/2$ when we take $B:=H$ and $H$ is sufficiently large. Thus, computing $\argmax_{y_{1:H}\in\mathcal{V}^{H}}\pi_{\theta}(y_{1:H}\mid{}\perp)$ yields a max-cut of $G$. It is well-known that computing a max-cut in a graph is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard, and the assumption that $G$ has an odd number of edges is without loss of generality. ∎

sections.title: E.2 Representational Challenges
path: Appendix E Computational and Representational Challenges in Sharpening

paragraphs.text: To give provable guarantees for our sharpening algorithms, we required certain realizability assumptions, which in particular posited that the model class actually contains a “sharpened” version of $\pi_{\texttt{base}}$ (Sections 4.1 and 4.2.1). In the simple example of a single-layer linear softmax model classes (corresponding to $H=1$ in the above definition), Section 4.2.1 is in fact satisfied, and the sharpened model can be obtained by increasing the temperature of $\pi_{\texttt{base}}$. However, multi-layer linear softmax models with $H\gg 1$ are more realistic. The following proposition shows that as soon as $H\geq 2$, multi-layer linear softmax model classes may not be closed under sharpening. This illustrates a potential drawback of training-time sharpening compared to inference-time sharpening, which requires no realizability assumptions. It also provides a simple example where greedy decoding does not yield a sequence-level arg-max response (since increasing temperature in a multi-layer softmax model class exactly converges to the greedy decoding).

Let $\mathcal{X}=\{\perp\}$, $\mathcal{V}=[n]$, and $H=d=2$. For any $n$ sufficiently large, there is a multi-layer linear softmax policy class $\Pi_{\phi,B,H}$ and a policy $\pi_{\texttt{base}}\in\Pi_{\phi,B,H}$ such that $y^{\star}_{1:H}:=\argmax_{y_{1:H}\in\mathcal{V}^{H}}\pi_{\theta}(y_{1:H}\mid{}\perp)$ is unique, but for all $B^{\prime}>B$ and $\pi\in\Pi_{\phi,B^{\prime},H}$, it holds that $\pi(y^{\star}_{1:H}\mid{}\perp)\leq 1/2$.
Proof of Section E.2. Throughout, we omit the dependence on the prompt $\perp$ for notational clarity. Since $H=2$, the model class consists of models $\pi_{\theta}$ of the form

\pi_{\theta}(a)=\pi_{\theta_{1}}(y_{1})\pi_{\theta_{2}}(y_{2}\mid{}y_{1})=\frac{\exp(\langle\phi_{1}(y_{1}),\theta_{1}\rangle)}{Z_{\theta_{1}}}\frac{\exp(\langle\phi_{2}(y_{1:2}),\theta_{2}\rangle)}{Z_{\theta_{2}}(y_{1})}\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:softmax-h2}

for $Z_{\theta_{1}}\vcentcolon={}\sum_{y_{1}\in\mathcal{V}}\exp(\langle\phi_{1}(y_{1}),\theta_{1}\rangle)$ and $Z_{\theta_{2}}(y_{1})\vcentcolon={}\sum_{y_{2}\in\mathcal{V}}\exp(\langle\phi_{2}(y_{1:2}),\theta_{2}\rangle)$.
Define $\phi_{1}$ by:
\phi_{1}(i)=\begin{cases}e_{1}&\text{ if }i=1\\ e_{1}&\text{ if }i=2\\ e_{2}&\text{ if }i\geq 3\end{cases}.
Define $\phi_{2}$ by:
\phi_{2}(i,j)=\begin{cases}e_{1}&\text{ if }i=2,j=1\\ e_{2}&\text{ if }i=2,j\neq 1\\ 0&\text{ if }i\neq 2\end{cases}.

Define $\pi_{\texttt{base}}:=\pi_{\theta^{\star}}$ where $\theta^{\star}_{1}:=\theta^{\star}_{2}:=B\cdot{}e_{1}$ for a parameter $B\geq\log(n)$. Then $\pi_{\texttt{base}}(1)=\pi_{\texttt{base}}(2)$ and $\pi_{\texttt{base}}(i)\leq e^{-B}\pi_{\texttt{base}}(2)$ for all $i\in\{3,\dots,n\}$. Moreover, $\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\cdot\mid{}i)=\mathsf{Unif}([n])$ for all $i\neq 2$, and $\pi_{\texttt{base}}(j\mid{}2)\leq e^{-B}\pi_{\texttt{base}}(1\mid{}2)$ for all $j\neq 1$. Thus,
\pi_{\texttt{base}}(2,1)=\pi_{\texttt{base}}(2)\pi_{\texttt{base}}(1\mid{}2)\geq\frac{1}{2+(n-2)e^{-B}}\cdot\frac{1}{1+(n-1)e^{-B}}\geq\Omega(1)

whereas $\pi_{\texttt{base}}(i,j)=O(1/n)$ for all $(i,j)\neq(2,1)$. Thus, $(2,1)$ is the sequence-level argmax for sufficiently large $n$. However, for any $\pi_{\theta}$ of the form described in Eq. 42, we have
\pi_{\theta}(2,1)\leq\pi_{\theta}(2)\leq\frac{\pi_{\theta}(2)}{\pi_{\theta}(1)+\pi_{\theta}(2)}=\frac{1}{2}

since $\phi(1)=\phi(2)$. This means that there is no $B^{\prime}$ for which $\Pi_{\phi,B^{\prime},H}$ contains an $(\epsilon,\delta)$-sharpened policy for $\pi_{\texttt{base}}$ for any $\delta>1/2$. ∎

sections.title: F.1 Guarantees for Approximate Maximizers

paragraphs.text: Recall that the theoretical guarantees for sharpening algorithms in Section 4 provide convergence to the set $\bm{y}^{\star}(x)\vcentcolon={}\argmax_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x)$ of (potentially non-unique) maximizers for the maximum-likelihood sharpening self-reward function $\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x)$. These guarantees require that the base model $\pi_{\texttt{base}}$ places sufficient provability mass on $\bm{y}^{\star}(x)$, which may not always be realistic. To address this, throughout this appendix we state and prove more general versions of our theoretical results that allow for approximate maximizers, and consequently enjoy weaker coverage assumptions
For a parameter $\gamma\in[0,1)$ we define
\displaystyle\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\vcentcolon={}\left\{y\mid{}\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x)\geq{}(1-\gamma)\cdot\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid x)\right\}

as the set of $(1-\gamma)$-approximate maximizers for $\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x)$. We quantify the quality of a sharpened model as follows. [Sharpened model] We say that a model $\widehat{\pi}$ is $(\epsilon,\delta,\gamma)$-sharpened relative to $\pi_{\texttt{base}}$ if
\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[\widehat{\pi}\left(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x\right)\geq{}1-\delta\right]\geq{}1-\epsilon.
That is, an $(\epsilon,\delta,\gamma)$-sharpened policy places at least $1-\delta$ mass on $(1-\gamma)$-approximate arg-max responses on all but an $\epsilon$-fraction of prompts under $\mu$.
Lastly, we will make use of the following generalized coverage coefficient
\displaystyle C_{\texttt{cov},\gamma}=\En_{x\sim\mu}\left[\frac{1}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)}\right],
which has $C_{\texttt{cov},\gamma}\leq{}C_{\texttt{cov}}$.

sections.title: F.2 Technical Tools

paragraphs.text: For a pair of probability measures $\mathbb{P}$ and $\mathbb{Q}$ with a common dominating measure $\omega$, Hellinger distance is defined via

\displaystyle D^{2}_{\mathsf{H}}\left(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q}\right)=\int\left(\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}}{\mathrm{d}\omega}}-\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbb{Q}}{\mathrm{d}\omega}}\right)^{2}\mathrm{d}\omega.

[MLE for conditional density estimation (e.g., Wong and Shen (1995); van de Geer (2000); Zhang (2006))] Consider a conditional density $\pi^{\star}:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\Delta(\mathcal{Y})$. Let $\mathcal{D}=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}$ be a dataset in which $(x_{i},y_{i})$ are drawn i.i.d. as $x_{i}\sim\mu\in\Delta(\mathcal{X})$ and $y_{i}\sim\pi^{\star}(\cdot\mid{}x)$. Suppose we have a finite function class $\Pi\subset(\mathcal{X}\to\Delta(\mathcal{Y}))$ such that $\pi^{\star}\in\Pi$. Define the maximum likelihood estimator
\displaystyle\widehat{\pi}\vcentcolon=\argmax_{\pi\in\Pi}\sum_{(x,y)\in\mathcal{D}}\log\pi(y\mid{}x).
Then with probability at least $1-\rho$,
\displaystyle\En_{x\sim\mu}\left[D^{2}_{\mathsf{H}}\left(\widehat{\pi}(\cdot\mid{}x),\pi^{\star}(\cdot\mid{}x)\right)\right]\leq\frac{2\log(|\Pi|\rho^{-1})}{n}.

[Elliptic potential lemma] Let $\lambda,K>0$, and let $A_{1},\dots,A_{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ be positive semi-definite matrices with $\Tr(A_{t})\leq K$ for all $t\in[T]$. Fix $\Gamma_{0}=\lambda I_{d}$ and $\Gamma_{t}=\lambda I_{d}+\sum_{i=1}^{t}A_{i}$ for $t\in[T]$. Then
\sum_{t=1}^{T}\Tr(\Gamma_{t-1}^{-1}A_{t})\leq\frac{dK\log\frac{(T+1)K}{\lambda}}{\lambda\log(1+K/\lambda)}.

Proof of Section F.2. Fix $t\in[T]$. Since $\Tr(A_{t})\leq 1$, there is some $p_{t}\in\Delta(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ such that $A_{t}=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim p_{t}}[aa^{\top}]$ and $\mathbb{P}[\lVert a\rVert_{2}\leq 1]=1$. Now observe that

\displaystyle\log\det(\Gamma_{t}) \displaystyle=\log\det(\Gamma_{t-1}+A_{t}) \displaystyle=\log\det(\Gamma_{t-1})+\log\det(I_{d}+\Gamma_{t-1}^{-1/2}A_{t}\Gamma_{t-1}^{-1/2}) \displaystyle=\log\det(\Gamma_{t-1})+\log\det\left(\mathbb{E}_{a\sim p_{t}}\left[I_{d}+\Gamma_{t-1}^{-1/2}aa^{\top}\Gamma_{t-1}^{-1/2}\right]\right) \displaystyle\geq\log\det(\Gamma_{t-1})+\mathbb{E}_{a\sim p_{t}}\log\det(I_{d}+\Gamma_{t-1}^{-1/2}aa^{\top}\Gamma_{t-1}^{-1/2}) \displaystyle=\log\det(\Gamma_{t-1})+\mathbb{E}_{a\sim p_{t}}\log(1+a^{\top}\Gamma_{t-1}^{-1}a).

Now $a^{\top}\Gamma_{t-1}^{-1}a\leq 1/\lambda$ with probability $1$, where $\lambda=\lambda_{\min}(\Gamma_{0})$. We know that $\lambda x\log(1+1/\lambda)\leq\log(1+x)$ for all $x\in[0,1/\lambda]$. Thus,
\log\det(\Gamma_{t})\geq\log\det(\Gamma_{t-1})+\lambda\log(1+1/\lambda)\mathbb{E}_{a\sim p_{t}}a^{\top}\Gamma_{t-1}^{-1}a.
Summing over $t\in[T]$, we get
\log\det(\Gamma_{T})\geq\log\det(\Gamma_{0})+\lambda\log(1+1/\lambda)\sum_{t=1}^{T}\Tr(\Gamma_{t-1}^{-1}A_{t}).
Finally note that $\lambda_{\max}(\Gamma_{T})\leq T+1$ so $\log\det(\Gamma_{T})\leq d\log T$, whereas $\log\det(\Gamma_{0})\geq d\log\lambda$. Thus,
\sum_{t=1}^{T}\Tr(\Gamma_{t-1}^{-1}A_{t})\leq\frac{d\log\frac{T+1}{\lambda}}{\lambda\log(1+1/\lambda)}
as claimed. ∎

[Freedman’s inequality, e.g. Agarwal et al. (2014)] Let $(Z_{t})_{t=1}^{T}$ be a martingale difference sequence adapted to filtration $(\mathcal{F}_{t})_{t=0}^{T-1}$. Suppose that $|Z_{t}|\leq R$ holds almost surely for all $t$. For any $\delta\in(0,1)$ and $\eta\in(0,1/R)$, it holds with probability at least $1-\delta$ that
\sum_{t=1}^{T}Z_{t}\leq\eta\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[Z_{t}^{2}|\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]+\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{\eta}.

Let $(Z_{t})_{t=1}^{T}$ be a sequence of random variables adapted to filtration $(\mathcal{F}_{t})_{t=0}^{T-1}$. Suppose that $Z_{t}\in[0,R]$ holds almost surely for all $t$. For any $\delta\in(0,1)$, it holds with probability at least $1-\delta$ that
\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[Z_{t}|\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]\leq 2\sum_{t=1}^{T}Z_{t}+4R\log(1/\delta).
Proof of Section F.2. Observe that for any $t\in[T]$,

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(Z_{t}-\mathbb{E}[Z_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}])^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}] \displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}[Z_{t}^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}] \displaystyle\leq R\cdot\mathbb{E}[Z_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}].

Applying Section F.2 to the sequence $(\mathbb{E}[Z_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]-Z_{t})_{t=1}^{T}$, which is a martingale difference sequence with elements supported almost surely on $[-R,R]$, we get for any $\eta\in(0,1/R)$ that with probability at least $1-\delta$,

\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}(\mathbb{E}[Z_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]-Z_{t}) \displaystyle\leq\eta\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[(Z_{t}-\mathbb{E}[Z_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}])^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]+\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{\eta} \displaystyle\leq\eta R\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[Z_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]+\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{\eta}.
Set $\eta=1/(2R)$. Simplifying gives
\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[Z_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]\leq 2\sum_{t=1}^{T}Z_{t}+4R\log(1/\delta).
as claimed. ∎

Suppose that $|Z_{t}|\leq R$ holds almost surely for all $t$. For any $\delta\in(0,1)$ and $\eta\in(0,1/R)$, it holds with probability at least $1-\delta$ that

\sum_{t=1}^{T}Z_{t}\leq\eta\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[Z_{t}^{2}|\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]+\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{\eta}.

Let $(Z_{t})_{t=1}^{T}$ be a sequence of random variables adapted to filtration $(\mathcal{F}_{t})_{t=0}^{T-1}$. Suppose that $Z_{t}\in[0,R]$ holds almost surely for all $t$. For any $\delta\in(0,1)$, it holds with probability at least $1-\delta$ that

\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[Z_{t}|\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]\leq 2\sum_{t=1}^{T}Z_{t}+4R\log(1/\delta).

Proof of Section F.2. Observe that for any $t\in[T]$,

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(Z_{t}-\mathbb{E}[Z_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}])^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}] \displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}[Z_{t}^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}] \displaystyle\leq R\cdot\mathbb{E}[Z_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}].

Applying Section F.2 to the sequence $(\mathbb{E}[Z_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]-Z_{t})_{t=1}^{T}$, which is a martingale difference sequence with elements supported almost surely on $[-R,R]$, we get for any $\eta\in(0,1/R)$ that with probability at least $1-\delta$,

\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}(\mathbb{E}[Z_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]-Z_{t}) \displaystyle\leq\eta\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[(Z_{t}-\mathbb{E}[Z_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}])^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]+\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{\eta} \displaystyle\leq\eta R\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[Z_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]+\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{\eta}.

Set $\eta=1/(2R)$. Simplifying gives

\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[Z_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]\leq 2\sum_{t=1}^{T}Z_{t}+4R\log(1/\delta).

as claimed. ∎

sections.title: Appendix G Proofs from Section 3.1

paragraphs.text: Proof of Section 3.1. We prove the result by induction. Fix $x\in\mathcal{X}$, and let $y^{\star}_{1},\ldots,y^{\star}_{H}\vcentcolon={}y^{\star}(x)$. Fix $h\in[H]$, and assume by induction that $\widehat{y}_{h^{\prime}}=y^{\star}_{h^{\prime}}$ for all $h^{\prime}<h$. We claim that in this case,
\displaystyle\pi_{h}(y^{\star}_{h}\mid{}\widehat{y}_{1},\ldots,\widehat{y}_{h-1},x)=\pi_{h}(y^{\star}_{h}\mid{}y^{\star}_{1},\ldots,y^{\star}_{h-1},x)>1/2,
which implies that $\widehat{y}_{h}=y^{\star}_{h}$. To see this, we observe that by Bayes’ rule,

\displaystyle\pi(y^{\star}_{1},\ldots,y^{\star}_{H}\mid{}x) \displaystyle\leq{}\pi(y^{\star}_{1},\ldots,y^{\star}_{h}\mid{}x) \displaystyle=\prod_{h^{\prime}=1}^{h}\pi_{h^{\prime}}(y^{\star}_{h^{\prime}}\mid{}y^{\star}_{1},\ldots,y^{\star}_{h^{\prime}-1},x)\leq{}\pi_{h}(y^{\star}_{h}\mid{}y^{\star}_{1},\ldots,y^{\star}_{h-1},x).

If we were to have $\pi_{h}(y^{\star}_{h}\mid{}\widehat{y}_{1},\ldots,\widehat{y}_{h-1},x)=\pi_{h}(y^{\star}_{h}\mid{}y^{\star}_{1},\ldots,y^{\star}_{h-1},x)\leq{}1/2$, it would contradict the assumption that $\pi(y^{\star}_{1},\ldots,y^{\star}_{H}\mid{}x)>1/2$. This proves the result. ∎

sections.title: Appendix H Proofs from Section 3.3

paragraphs.text: Below, we state and prove a generalization of Sections 3.3 and D which allows for approximate maximizers in the sense of Section F.1, as well as a more general coverage coefficient.
To state the result, for a model $\pi$, we define
\displaystyle\bm{y}^{\pi}_{\gamma}(x)=\left\{y\mid{}\pi(y\mid{}x)\geq{}(1-\gamma)\cdot\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi(y\mid x)\right\}.
Next, for any integer $p\in\mathbb{N}$, we define
\displaystyle C_{\texttt{cov},\gamma,p}(\pi)=\left(\En\left[\frac{1}{(\pi(\bm{y}^{\pi}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x))^{p}}\right]\right)^{1/p},

with the convention that $C_{\texttt{cov},\gamma,p}=C_{\texttt{cov},\gamma,p}(\pi_{\texttt{base}})$. Our most general lower bound, Appendix H, holds in the regime where $\gamma=1/2$, and thus the best response$y$ has bounded margin away from suboptimal responses. [Lower bound for sharpening] Fix integers $d\geq 1$ and $p\geq 1$ and parameters $\epsilon\in(0,1)$ and $C\geq 1$, and set $\gamma=1/2$. There exists a class of models $\Pi$ such that i) $\log|\Pi|\asymp d(1+\log(C\epsilon^{-1/p}))$, ii) $\sup_{\pi\in\Pi}C_{\texttt{cov},\gamma,p}(\pi)\lesssim C$, and iii) $\bm{y}^{\pi}_{\gamma}(x)$ is a singleton for all $\pi\in\Pi$, for which any sharpening algorithm $\widehat{\pi}$ that attains $\En\left[\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}[\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\pi_{\texttt{base}}}_{\gamma}(x))>1/2]\right]\geq 1-\epsilon$ for all $\pi_{\texttt{base}}\in\Pi$ must collect a total number of samples $m=n\cdot{}N$ at least

\displaystyle m\gtrsim\begin{cases}\frac{C\log|\Pi|}{\epsilon^{1+1/p}(1+\log(C\epsilon^{-1/p}))}&\text{sample-and-evaluate oracle},\\ \frac{C\log|\Pi|}{\epsilon^{1/p}(1+\log(C\epsilon^{-1/p}))}&\text{adaptive sample-and-evaluate oracle}.\end{cases}
Proof of Appendix H

Let parameters $d,p\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\epsilon>0$ be given, and set $\gamma=1/2$. Let $M\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\Delta>0$ be parameters to be chosen later. Let $\mathcal{X}=\{x_{0},x_{1},\dots,x_{d}\}$ and $\mathcal{Y}=\{y_{0},y_{1},\dots,y_{M}\}$ be arbitrary discrete sets (with $\lvert\mathcal{X}\rvert=d+1$ and $\lvert\mathcal{Y}\rvert=M+1$).
Construction of prompt distribution and model class
We use the same construction for the non-adaptive and adaptive lower bounds in the theorem statement. We define the prompt distribution $\mu$ via
\displaystyle\mu:=(1-\Delta)\updelta_{x_{0}}+\frac{\Delta}{d}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\updelta_{x_{i}},
where $\updelta_{x}$ denotes the Dirac delta distribution on element $x$.
As the first step toward constructing the model class $\Pi$, we introduce a family of distributions $(P_{0},P_{1},\dots,P_{M})$ on $\mathcal{Y}$ as follows

\displaystyle P_{0}=\updelta_{y_{0}},\quad\forall i\geq 1,~P_{i}=\frac{1}{(1-\gamma)M}\updelta_{y_{i}}+\sum_{j\in[M]\setminus\{i\}}\frac{1}{M}\left(1-\frac{\gamma}{(M-1)(1-\gamma)}\right)\updelta_{y_{j}}.
Next, for or any index $\mathcal{I}=(j_{1},j_{2},\dots,j_{d})\in[M]^{d}$, define a model
\displaystyle\pi^{\mathcal{I}}(x_{i})=\begin{cases}P_{0}&i=0\\ P_{j_{i}}&i>0\end{cases}.
We define the model class as
\displaystyle\Pi:=\{\pi^{\mathcal{I}}:\mathcal{I}\in[M]^{d}\},
which we note has
\displaystyle\log|\Pi| \displaystyle=d\log M.
Preliminary technical results
Define
\displaystyle\bm{y}^{\mathcal{I}}_{\gamma}(x):=\{y:\pi^{\mathcal{I}}(y\mid x)\geq(1-\gamma)\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi^{\mathcal{I}}(y\mid{}x)\}.

The following property is immediate. Let $\mathcal{I}=(j_{1},\dots,j_{d})\in[d]^{M}$. Then $\bm{y}^{\mathcal{I}}_{\gamma}(x_{i})=\{y_{j_{i}}\}$ if $i>0$, and $\bm{y}^{\mathcal{I}}_{\gamma}(x_{0})=\{y_{0}\}$. In view of this result, we define $y^{\mathcal{I}}(x)=\argmax_{y}\pi^{\mathcal{I}}(y\mid{}x)$ as the unique arg-max response for $x$.

Going forward, let us fix the algorithm under consideration. Let $\mathbb{P}^{\mathcal{I}}[\cdot]$ denote the law over the dataset used by the algorithm when the true instance is $\pi^{\mathcal{I}}$ (including possible randomness and adaptivity from the algorithm itself), and let $\En^{\mathcal{I}}[\cdot]$ denote the corresponding expectation. The following lemma is a basic technical result. [Reduction to classification] Let $\widehat{\pi}$ be the model produced by an algorithm with access to a (adaptive) sample-and-evaluate oracle for $\pi^{\mathcal{I}}$. Suppose that for some $\epsilon\geq{}0$,
\displaystyle\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}[\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\mathcal{I}}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)>1/2]\geq 1-\epsilon.

Define $\widehat{\mathcal{I}}=(\widehat{j}_{1},\dots,\widehat{j}_{d})$ via $\widehat{j}_{i}=\argmax_{j}\widehat{\pi}(y_{j}\mid x_{i})$, and write $\mathcal{I}=(j_{1}^{\star},\dots,j_{d}^{\star})$. Then,
\displaystyle\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{j}_{i}\neq j_{i}^{\star}\}\right]\leq\epsilon/\Delta.

Proof of Appendix H. As established in Appendix H, under instance $\mathcal{I}$, $\bm{y}^{\mathcal{I}}_{\gamma}(x_{i})=\{y_{j_{i}^{\star}}\}$ for any $i\in[d]$. Thus, whenever $\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\mathcal{I}}_{\gamma}(x_{i}))>1/2$, $j_{i}^{\star}=\argmax_{j}\widehat{\pi}(y_{j}\mid x_{i})=:\widehat{j}_{i}$. The result follows by noting that the event $\{\exists i\in[d]:x=x_{i}\}$ occurs with probability at least $\Delta$ under $x\sim\mu$. ∎
Lower bound under sample-and-evaluate oracle

Recall that in the non-adaptive framework, the sample complexity $m$ is fixed. In light of Appendix H, it suffices to establishes the following claim. There exists a universal constant $c>0$ such that for all $M\geq 8$, if $m\leq cdM/\Delta$, then $\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{j}_{i}\neq j_{i}^{\star}\}\right]\geq 1/8$ for all $i$. With this, the result follows by selecting $\Delta=16\epsilon$, with which Appendix H implies that any algorithm with $\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}[\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\mathcal{I}}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)>1/2]\geq{}1-\epsilon$ must have $m\gtrsim dM/\Delta$. To conclude, we choose $M\asymp 1+C\epsilon^{-1/p}$, which gives $m\asymp dM/\Delta\asymp dC\epsilon^{-(1+1/p)}\asymp\epsilon^{-(1+1/p)}\log\Pi/\log(1+C\epsilon^{1/p})$. Finally, we check that with this choice, all $\pi\in\Pi$ satisfy

\displaystyle C_{\texttt{cov},\gamma,p}(\pi) \displaystyle=\left(\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[x=x_{0}\right]+\left(M(1-\gamma)\right)^{p}\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[x\neq x_{0}\right]\right)^{1/p} \displaystyle=\left((1-\Delta)+\left(M(1-\gamma)\right)^{p}\Delta\right)^{1/p} \displaystyle\lesssim\left((1-\Delta)+\left(8C(1-\gamma)\right)^{p}\right)^{1/p}\lesssim C.

Proof of Appendix H. Let $i\in[d]$ be fixed. Of the $m=n\cdot{}N$ tuples $(x,y,\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x))$ that are observed by the algorithm, let $m_{i}$ denote the (random) number of such examples for which $x=x_{i}$. From Markov’s inequality, we have
\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[m_{i}\leq 2\Delta m/d]\geq\frac{1}{2}

Going forward, let $\mathcal{D}=\left\{(x,y,\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x))\right\}$ denote the dataset collected by the algorithm, which has $\lvert\mathcal{D}\rvert=m$. Let $\mathcal{E}_{i}$ denote the event that, for prompt $x=x_{i}$, (i) there are at least two distinct responses $y_{j}$ for which $(x_{i},y_{j})\notin\mathcal{D}$; and (ii) there are no pairs $(x_{i},y)\in\mathcal{D}$ for which $\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x_{i})>\frac{1}{M}$. Since $\mathcal{E}_{i}$ is a measurable function of $\mathcal{D}$, we can write

where $\mathcal{I}\sim\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{I}=\cdot\mid\mathcal{D}]$ is sampled from the posterior distribution over $\mathcal{I}$ conditioned on the dataset $\mathcal{D}$. Observe that conditioned on $\mathcal{E}_{i}$, the posterior distribution over $j_{i}^{\star}$ under $\mathcal{I}\sim\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{I}=\cdot\mid\mathcal{D}]$ is uniform over the set of indices $j\in[M]$ for which $(x_{i},y_{j})\notin\mathcal{D}$, and this set has size at least $2$. Hence, $\mathbb{I}\{\mathcal{E}_{i}\}\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{I}=\cdot\mid\mathcal{D}]}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{j}_{i}\neq j^{\star}_{i}\}\right]\geq\frac{1}{2}$, and resuming from Eq. 88, we have

\displaystyle\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{j}_{i}\neq j_{i}^{\star}\}\right]\geq\frac{1}{2}\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\mathcal{E}_{i}\}\right] \displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{2}\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\mathbb{P}^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathcal{E}_{i}\cap\{m_{i}\leq 2\Delta m/d\}\right] \displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{4}\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\mathbb{P}^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathcal{E}_{i}\mid m_{i}\leq 2\Delta m/d\right],

where the last inequality is from Eq. 86. Finally, we can check that under the law $\mathbb{P}^{\mathcal{I}}$, the probability of the event $\mathcal{E}_{i}$—conditioned on the value $m_{i}$—is at least the probability that $(x_{i},y_{j^{\star}_{i}}),(x_{i},y_{j^{\prime}})\notin\mathcal{D}$ for an arbitrary fixed index $j^{\prime}\neq j^{\star}_{i}$, which on the event $\{m_{i}\leq 2\Delta{}m/d\}$ is at least
\displaystyle\left(1-\frac{3}{M}\right)^{m_{i}}\geq\left(1-\frac{3}{M}\right)^{2\Delta m/d},

where we have used that $\gamma=1/2$. The value above is at least $\frac{1}{4}$ whenever $m\leq c\cdot{}dM/\Delta$ for a sufficiently small absolute constant $c>0$. For this value of $m$, we conclude that $\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{j}_{i}\neq j_{i}^{\star}\}\right]\geq\frac{1}{4}\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\mathbb{P}^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathcal{E}_{i}\mid\{m_{i}\leq 2\Delta m/d\}\right]\geq\frac{1}{8}$. ∎
Lower bound under adaptive sample-and-evaluate oracle

In the adaptive framework, we let $m_{i}$ denote the (potentially random) number of tuples $(x,y,\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x))$ observed by the algorithm in which $x=x_{i}$. Note that unlike the non-adaptive framework, the distribution over $m_{i}$ depends on the underlying instance $\mathcal{I}$ with which the algorithm interacts.

To begin, from Appendix H and Markov’s inequality, if $\widehat{\pi}$ satisfies the guarantee $\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}[\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\mathcal{I}}_{\gamma}(x))>1/2]\geq 1-\epsilon$, then there exists a set of indices $S_{\texttt{good}}\subset[d]$ such that
Footnote: 14 14 We emphasize that the set $S_{\texttt{good}}$ is not a random variable, and depends only on the algorithm itself.

\displaystyle|S_{\texttt{good}}|\geq\lfloor d/2\rfloor,\quad\forall i\in S_{\texttt{good}},~\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{j}_{i}\neq j_{i}^{\star}\}\right]\leq\frac{2\epsilon}{\Delta}.
We now appeal to the following lemma. As long as $M\geq{}6$, it holds that for all $i\in[d]$,

\displaystyle\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{j}_{i}\neq j_{i}^{\star}\}\right]\geq{}\frac{1}{4e}\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{m_{i}\leq{}M/3\}\right].
Combining Appendix H with Eq. 92, it follows that there exist absolute constant $c_{1},c_{2},c_{3}>0$ such that if $\Delta=c_{1}\cdot{}\epsilon$, then for all $i\in S_{\texttt{good}}$,
\displaystyle\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\mathbb{P}^{\mathcal{I}}\left[m_{i}\geq{}c_{2}M\right]\geq{}c_{3}.
Thus, with this choice for $\Delta$, we have that $i\in S_{\texttt{good}}$,
\displaystyle\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[m_{i}\right]\gtrsim M,
and we can lower bound the algorithm’s expected sample complexity by summing over $i\in S_{\texttt{good}}$:

\displaystyle\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[m\right]\geq\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\sum_{i\in S_{\texttt{good}}}m_{i}\right]\gtrsim|S_{\texttt{good}}|M\gtrsim dM.

The result now follows by tuning $M\asymp 1+C\epsilon^{-1/p}$ as in the proof of the lower bound for non-adaptive sampling, which gives $\En[m]\gtrsim{}dM\asymp dC\epsilon^{-1/p}\asymp\epsilon^{-1/p}\log\Pi/\log(1+C\epsilon^{1/p})$ and $C_{\texttt{cov},\gamma,p}(\pi)\lesssim{}C$ for all $\pi\in\Pi$.

Proof of Appendix H. Let $i\in[d]$ be fixed. Let $\mathcal{D}=\left\{(x,y,\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x))\right\}$ denote the dataset collected by the algorithm at termination, which has $\lvert\mathcal{D}\rvert=m$. Let $\mathcal{E}_{i}$ denote the event that, for prompt $x=x_{i}$, (i) there are at least two distinct responses $y_{j}$ for which $(x_{i},y_{j})\notin\mathcal{D}$; and (ii) there are no pairs $(x_{i},y)\in\mathcal{D}$ for which $\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x_{i})>\frac{1}{M}$. Since $\mathcal{E}_{i}$ is a measurable function of $\mathcal{D}$, we can write

where $\mathcal{I}\sim\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{I}=\cdot\mid\mathcal{D}]$ is sampled from the posterior distribution over $\mathcal{I}$ conditioned on the dataset $\mathcal{D}$. Observe that conditioned on $\mathcal{E}_{i}$, the posterior distribution over $j_{i}^{\star}$ under $\mathcal{I}\sim\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{I}=\cdot\mid\mathcal{D}]$ is uniform over the set of indices $j\in[M]$ for which $(x_{i},y_{j})\notin\mathcal{D}$, and this set has size at least $2$. Hence, $\mathbb{I}\{\mathcal{E}_{i}\}\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{I}=\cdot\mid\mathcal{D}]}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{j}_{i}\neq j^{\star}_{i}\}\right]\geq\frac{1}{2}$, and resuming from Eq. 98, we have

\displaystyle\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{j}_{i}\neq j_{i}^{\star}\}\right] \displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{2}\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\mathcal{E}_{i}\}\right] \displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{2}\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\mathbb{P}^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathcal{E}_{i}\cap\{m_{i}\leq M/3\}\right] \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\left[\mathbb{P}^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathcal{E}_{i}\mid m_{i}\leq M/3\right]\cdot\mathbb{P}^{\mathcal{I}}\left[m_{i}\leq{}M/3\right]\right].

The event $\mathcal{E}_{i}$ is a superset of the event $\mathcal{E}_{i,j^{\prime}}$ that $(x_{i},y_{j^{\star}_{i}}),(x_{i},y_{j^{\prime}})\notin\mathcal{D}$ for an arbitrary fixed index $j^{\prime}\neq j^{\star}_{i}$. Thus,
\displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathcal{E}_{i}\mid m_{i}\leq M/3\right]\geq\mathbb{P}^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathcal{E}_{i,j^{\prime}}\mid m_{i}\leq M/3\right]

Moreover, we can realize the law of $\mathbb{P}^{\mathcal{I}}$ considering an infinite tape, associated to index $i$, of i.i.d. samples $y\sim\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\cdot\mid x_{i})$, and taking the first $m_{i}$ elements on this tape to be the samples $(x,y,\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid x))\in\mathcal{D}$ with $x=x_{i}$ (see, e.g. Simchowitz et al. (2017) for an argument of this form). On the event $\{m_{i}\leq M/3\}$, the $m_{i}$ samples in $(x,y,\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid x))\in\mathcal{D}$ with $x=x_{i}$ are a subset of the first $M/3$ samples from the index-$i$ tape. Viewed in this way, we can lower bound the probability of $\mathcal{E}_{i,j}$ by the probability of the event $\tilde{}\mathcal{E}_{i,j^{\prime}}$ that the first $M/3$ $y$’s on the index-$i$ tape contain neither $j^{\star}_{i}$, nor the designated index $j^{\prime}$. As these first $M/3$ $y$’s are not chosen adaptively, the probability of $\tilde{}\mathcal{E}_{i,j^{\prime}}$ is at least
\displaystyle\left(1-\frac{3}{M}\right)^{m_{i}}\geq\left(1-\frac{3}{M}\right)^{M/3}\geq\frac{1}{2e},
as long as $M\geq{}6$ and $\gamma=1/2$. We conclude that

\displaystyle\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{j}_{i}\neq j_{i}^{\star}\}\right]\geq{}\frac{1}{4e}\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{m_{i}\leq{}M/3\}\right].

Preliminary technical results

Define

\displaystyle\bm{y}^{\mathcal{I}}_{\gamma}(x):=\{y:\pi^{\mathcal{I}}(y\mid x)\geq(1-\gamma)\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi^{\mathcal{I}}(y\mid{}x)\}.

The following property is immediate. Let $\mathcal{I}=(j_{1},\dots,j_{d})\in[d]^{M}$. Then $\bm{y}^{\mathcal{I}}_{\gamma}(x_{i})=\{y_{j_{i}}\}$ if $i>0$, and $\bm{y}^{\mathcal{I}}_{\gamma}(x_{0})=\{y_{0}\}$. In view of this result, we define $y^{\mathcal{I}}(x)=\argmax_{y}\pi^{\mathcal{I}}(y\mid{}x)$ as the unique arg-max response for $x$.

Going forward, let us fix the algorithm under consideration. Let $\mathbb{P}^{\mathcal{I}}[\cdot]$ denote the law over the dataset used by the algorithm when the true instance is $\pi^{\mathcal{I}}$ (including possible randomness and adaptivity from the algorithm itself), and let $\En^{\mathcal{I}}[\cdot]$ denote the corresponding expectation. The following lemma is a basic technical result. [Reduction to classification] Let $\widehat{\pi}$ be the model produced by an algorithm with access to a (adaptive) sample-and-evaluate oracle for $\pi^{\mathcal{I}}$. Suppose that for some $\epsilon\geq{}0$,

\displaystyle\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}[\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\mathcal{I}}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)>1/2]\geq 1-\epsilon.

Define $\widehat{\mathcal{I}}=(\widehat{j}_{1},\dots,\widehat{j}_{d})$ via $\widehat{j}_{i}=\argmax_{j}\widehat{\pi}(y_{j}\mid x_{i})$, and write $\mathcal{I}=(j_{1}^{\star},\dots,j_{d}^{\star})$. Then,

\displaystyle\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{j}_{i}\neq j_{i}^{\star}\}\right]\leq\epsilon/\Delta.

Proof of Appendix H. As established in Appendix H, under instance $\mathcal{I}$, $\bm{y}^{\mathcal{I}}_{\gamma}(x_{i})=\{y_{j_{i}^{\star}}\}$ for any $i\in[d]$. Thus, whenever $\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\mathcal{I}}_{\gamma}(x_{i}))>1/2$, $j_{i}^{\star}=\argmax_{j}\widehat{\pi}(y_{j}\mid x_{i})=:\widehat{j}_{i}$. The result follows by noting that the event $\{\exists i\in[d]:x=x_{i}\}$ occurs with probability at least $\Delta$ under $x\sim\mu$. ∎

Lower bound under sample-and-evaluate oracle

Recall that in the non-adaptive framework, the sample complexity $m$ is fixed. In light of Appendix H, it suffices to establishes the following claim. There exists a universal constant $c>0$ such that for all $M\geq 8$, if $m\leq cdM/\Delta$, then $\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{j}_{i}\neq j_{i}^{\star}\}\right]\geq 1/8$ for all $i$. With this, the result follows by selecting $\Delta=16\epsilon$, with which Appendix H implies that any algorithm with $\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}[\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\mathcal{I}}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)>1/2]\geq{}1-\epsilon$ must have $m\gtrsim dM/\Delta$. To conclude, we choose $M\asymp 1+C\epsilon^{-1/p}$, which gives $m\asymp dM/\Delta\asymp dC\epsilon^{-(1+1/p)}\asymp\epsilon^{-(1+1/p)}\log\Pi/\log(1+C\epsilon^{1/p})$. Finally, we check that with this choice, all $\pi\in\Pi$ satisfy

\displaystyle C_{\texttt{cov},\gamma,p}(\pi) \displaystyle=\left(\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[x=x_{0}\right]+\left(M(1-\gamma)\right)^{p}\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[x\neq x_{0}\right]\right)^{1/p} \displaystyle=\left((1-\Delta)+\left(M(1-\gamma)\right)^{p}\Delta\right)^{1/p} \displaystyle\lesssim\left((1-\Delta)+\left(8C(1-\gamma)\right)^{p}\right)^{1/p}\lesssim C.

Proof of Appendix H. Let $i\in[d]$ be fixed. Of the $m=n\cdot{}N$ tuples $(x,y,\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x))$ that are observed by the algorithm, let $m_{i}$ denote the (random) number of such examples for which $x=x_{i}$. From Markov’s inequality, we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[m_{i}\leq 2\Delta m/d]\geq\frac{1}{2}

Going forward, let $\mathcal{D}=\left\{(x,y,\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x))\right\}$ denote the dataset collected by the algorithm, which has $\lvert\mathcal{D}\rvert=m$. Let $\mathcal{E}_{i}$ denote the event that, for prompt $x=x_{i}$, (i) there are at least two distinct responses $y_{j}$ for which $(x_{i},y_{j})\notin\mathcal{D}$; and (ii) there are no pairs $(x_{i},y)\in\mathcal{D}$ for which $\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x_{i})>\frac{1}{M}$. Since $\mathcal{E}_{i}$ is a measurable function of $\mathcal{D}$, we can write

\displaystyle\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{j}_{i}\neq j_{i}^{\star}\}\right] \displaystyle\geq\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{j}_{i}\neq j_{i}^{\star}\}\cdot\mathbb{I}\left\{\mathcal{E}_{i}\right\}\right] \displaystyle=\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\mathcal{E}_{i}\}\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{I}=\cdot\mid\mathcal{D}]}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{j}_{i}\neq j^{\star}_{i}\}\right]\right],

where $\mathcal{I}\sim\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{I}=\cdot\mid\mathcal{D}]$ is sampled from the posterior distribution over $\mathcal{I}$ conditioned on the dataset $\mathcal{D}$. Observe that conditioned on $\mathcal{E}_{i}$, the posterior distribution over $j_{i}^{\star}$ under $\mathcal{I}\sim\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{I}=\cdot\mid\mathcal{D}]$ is uniform over the set of indices $j\in[M]$ for which $(x_{i},y_{j})\notin\mathcal{D}$, and this set has size at least $2$. Hence, $\mathbb{I}\{\mathcal{E}_{i}\}\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{I}=\cdot\mid\mathcal{D}]}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{j}_{i}\neq j^{\star}_{i}\}\right]\geq\frac{1}{2}$, and resuming from Eq. 88, we have

\displaystyle\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{j}_{i}\neq j_{i}^{\star}\}\right]\geq\frac{1}{2}\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\mathcal{E}_{i}\}\right] \displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{2}\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\mathbb{P}^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathcal{E}_{i}\cap\{m_{i}\leq 2\Delta m/d\}\right] \displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{4}\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\mathbb{P}^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathcal{E}_{i}\mid m_{i}\leq 2\Delta m/d\right],

where the last inequality is from Eq. 86. Finally, we can check that under the law $\mathbb{P}^{\mathcal{I}}$, the probability of the event $\mathcal{E}_{i}$—conditioned on the value $m_{i}$—is at least the probability that $(x_{i},y_{j^{\star}_{i}}),(x_{i},y_{j^{\prime}})\notin\mathcal{D}$ for an arbitrary fixed index $j^{\prime}\neq j^{\star}_{i}$, which on the event $\{m_{i}\leq 2\Delta{}m/d\}$ is at least

\displaystyle\left(1-\frac{3}{M}\right)^{m_{i}}\geq\left(1-\frac{3}{M}\right)^{2\Delta m/d},

where we have used that $\gamma=1/2$. The value above is at least $\frac{1}{4}$ whenever $m\leq c\cdot{}dM/\Delta$ for a sufficiently small absolute constant $c>0$. For this value of $m$, we conclude that $\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{j}_{i}\neq j_{i}^{\star}\}\right]\geq\frac{1}{4}\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\mathbb{P}^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathcal{E}_{i}\mid\{m_{i}\leq 2\Delta m/d\}\right]\geq\frac{1}{8}$. ∎

Lower bound under adaptive sample-and-evaluate oracle

In the adaptive framework, we let $m_{i}$ denote the (potentially random) number of tuples $(x,y,\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x))$ observed by the algorithm in which $x=x_{i}$. Note that unlike the non-adaptive framework, the distribution over $m_{i}$ depends on the underlying instance $\mathcal{I}$ with which the algorithm interacts.

To begin, from Appendix H and Markov’s inequality, if $\widehat{\pi}$ satisfies the guarantee $\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}[\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\mathcal{I}}_{\gamma}(x))>1/2]\geq 1-\epsilon$, then there exists a set of indices $S_{\texttt{good}}\subset[d]$ such that

Footnote: 14 14 We emphasize that the set $S_{\texttt{good}}$ is not a random variable, and depends only on the algorithm itself.

\displaystyle|S_{\texttt{good}}|\geq\lfloor d/2\rfloor,\quad\forall i\in S_{\texttt{good}},~\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{j}_{i}\neq j_{i}^{\star}\}\right]\leq\frac{2\epsilon}{\Delta}.

We now appeal to the following lemma. As long as $M\geq{}6$, it holds that for all $i\in[d]$,

\displaystyle\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{j}_{i}\neq j_{i}^{\star}\}\right]\geq{}\frac{1}{4e}\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{m_{i}\leq{}M/3\}\right].

Combining Appendix H with Eq. 92, it follows that there exist absolute constant $c_{1},c_{2},c_{3}>0$ such that if $\Delta=c_{1}\cdot{}\epsilon$, then for all $i\in S_{\texttt{good}}$,

\displaystyle\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\mathbb{P}^{\mathcal{I}}\left[m_{i}\geq{}c_{2}M\right]\geq{}c_{3}.

Thus, with this choice for $\Delta$, we have that $i\in S_{\texttt{good}}$,

\displaystyle\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[m_{i}\right]\gtrsim M,

and we can lower bound the algorithm’s expected sample complexity by summing over $i\in S_{\texttt{good}}$:

\displaystyle\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[m\right]\geq\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\sum_{i\in S_{\texttt{good}}}m_{i}\right]\gtrsim|S_{\texttt{good}}|M\gtrsim dM.

The result now follows by tuning $M\asymp 1+C\epsilon^{-1/p}$ as in the proof of the lower bound for non-adaptive sampling, which gives $\En[m]\gtrsim{}dM\asymp dC\epsilon^{-1/p}\asymp\epsilon^{-1/p}\log\Pi/\log(1+C\epsilon^{1/p})$ and $C_{\texttt{cov},\gamma,p}(\pi)\lesssim{}C$ for all $\pi\in\Pi$.

Proof of Appendix H. Let $i\in[d]$ be fixed. Let $\mathcal{D}=\left\{(x,y,\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x))\right\}$ denote the dataset collected by the algorithm at termination, which has $\lvert\mathcal{D}\rvert=m$. Let $\mathcal{E}_{i}$ denote the event that, for prompt $x=x_{i}$, (i) there are at least two distinct responses $y_{j}$ for which $(x_{i},y_{j})\notin\mathcal{D}$; and (ii) there are no pairs $(x_{i},y)\in\mathcal{D}$ for which $\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x_{i})>\frac{1}{M}$. Since $\mathcal{E}_{i}$ is a measurable function of $\mathcal{D}$, we can write

\displaystyle\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{j}_{i}\neq j_{i}^{\star}\}\right] \displaystyle\geq\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{j}_{i}\neq j_{i}^{\star}\}\cdot\mathbb{I}\left\{\mathcal{E}_{i}\right\}\right] \displaystyle=\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\mathcal{E}_{i}\}\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{I}=\cdot\mid\mathcal{D}]}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{j}_{i}\neq j^{\star}_{i}\}\right]\right],

where $\mathcal{I}\sim\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{I}=\cdot\mid\mathcal{D}]$ is sampled from the posterior distribution over $\mathcal{I}$ conditioned on the dataset $\mathcal{D}$. Observe that conditioned on $\mathcal{E}_{i}$, the posterior distribution over $j_{i}^{\star}$ under $\mathcal{I}\sim\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{I}=\cdot\mid\mathcal{D}]$ is uniform over the set of indices $j\in[M]$ for which $(x_{i},y_{j})\notin\mathcal{D}$, and this set has size at least $2$. Hence, $\mathbb{I}\{\mathcal{E}_{i}\}\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{I}=\cdot\mid\mathcal{D}]}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{j}_{i}\neq j^{\star}_{i}\}\right]\geq\frac{1}{2}$, and resuming from Eq. 98, we have

\displaystyle\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{j}_{i}\neq j_{i}^{\star}\}\right] \displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{2}\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\mathcal{E}_{i}\}\right] \displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{2}\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\mathbb{P}^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathcal{E}_{i}\cap\{m_{i}\leq M/3\}\right] \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\left[\mathbb{P}^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathcal{E}_{i}\mid m_{i}\leq M/3\right]\cdot\mathbb{P}^{\mathcal{I}}\left[m_{i}\leq{}M/3\right]\right].

The event $\mathcal{E}_{i}$ is a superset of the event $\mathcal{E}_{i,j^{\prime}}$ that $(x_{i},y_{j^{\star}_{i}}),(x_{i},y_{j^{\prime}})\notin\mathcal{D}$ for an arbitrary fixed index $j^{\prime}\neq j^{\star}_{i}$. Thus,

\displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathcal{E}_{i}\mid m_{i}\leq M/3\right]\geq\mathbb{P}^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathcal{E}_{i,j^{\prime}}\mid m_{i}\leq M/3\right]

Moreover, we can realize the law of $\mathbb{P}^{\mathcal{I}}$ considering an infinite tape, associated to index $i$, of i.i.d. samples $y\sim\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\cdot\mid x_{i})$, and taking the first $m_{i}$ elements on this tape to be the samples $(x,y,\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid x))\in\mathcal{D}$ with $x=x_{i}$ (see, e.g. Simchowitz et al. (2017) for an argument of this form). On the event $\{m_{i}\leq M/3\}$, the $m_{i}$ samples in $(x,y,\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid x))\in\mathcal{D}$ with $x=x_{i}$ are a subset of the first $M/3$ samples from the index-$i$ tape. Viewed in this way, we can lower bound the probability of $\mathcal{E}_{i,j}$ by the probability of the event $\tilde{}\mathcal{E}_{i,j^{\prime}}$ that the first $M/3$ $y$’s on the index-$i$ tape contain neither $j^{\star}_{i}$, nor the designated index $j^{\prime}$. As these first $M/3$ $y$’s are not chosen adaptively, the probability of $\tilde{}\mathcal{E}_{i,j^{\prime}}$ is at least

\displaystyle\left(1-\frac{3}{M}\right)^{m_{i}}\geq\left(1-\frac{3}{M}\right)^{M/3}\geq\frac{1}{2e},

as long as $M\geq{}6$ and $\gamma=1/2$. We conclude that

\displaystyle\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{j}_{i}\neq j_{i}^{\star}\}\right]\geq{}\frac{1}{4e}\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{m_{i}\leq{}M/3\}\right].

∎

paragraphs.text: The following theorem is a generalization of Section 4.1 which allows for approximate maximizers in the sense of Section F.1. Let $\rho,\delta\in(0,1)$ be given, and suppose we set $N=N^{\star}\log(2\delta^{-1})$ for a parameter $N^{\star}\in\mathbb{N}$. Then for any $n\in\mathbb{N}$, SFT-Sharpening ensures that with probability at least $1-\rho$, for any $\gamma\in(0,1)$, the output model $\widehat{\pi}$ satisfies

\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)\leq{}1-2\delta\right]\lesssim{}\frac{1}{\delta}\cdot{}\frac{\log(\lvert\Pi\rvert\rho^{-1})}{n}+\frac{C_{\texttt{cov},\gamma}}{N^{\star}}.

In particular, given $(\epsilon,\delta,\gamma)$, by setting $n=C_{\ref{thm:bestofn}}\frac{\log\lvert\Pi\rvert}{\delta\epsilon}$ and $N^{\star}=C_{\ref{thm:bestofn}}\frac{C_{\texttt{cov},\gamma}}{\epsilon}$ for a sufficiently large absolute constant $C_{\ref{thm:bestofn}}>0$, we are guaranteed that
\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)\leq{}1-\delta\right]\leq\epsilon.
The total sample complexity is
\displaystyle m=O\left(\frac{C_{\texttt{cov},\gamma}\log(\lvert\Pi\rvert\rho^{-1})\log(\delta^{-1})}{\delta\epsilon^{2}}\right).
Proof of Appendix I. Under realizability of $\pi^{\texttt{BoN}}_{N}$ (Section 4.1), Section F.2 implies that the output of SFT-Sharpening satisfies, with probability at least $1-\rho$,

\displaystyle\En_{x\sim\mu}\left[D^{2}_{\mathsf{H}}\left(\widehat{\pi}(\cdot\mid{}x),\pi^{\texttt{BoN}}_{N}(\cdot\mid{}x)\right)\right]\leq\varepsilon_{\texttt{stat}}^{2}\vcentcolon={}\frac{2\log(\lvert\Pi\rvert/\rho)}{n}.
Henceforth we condition on the event that Eq. 108 holds. Let
\mathcal{X}_{\texttt{good}}\vcentcolon={}\left\{x\in\mathcal{X}\mid N^{\star}\geq\frac{1}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)}\right\}
denote the set of prompts for which $\pi_{\texttt{base}}$ places sufficiently high mass on $\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)$. We can bound

\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)\leq{}1-\delta\right] \displaystyle\qquad\leq{}\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)\leq{}1-\delta,x\in\mathcal{X}_{\texttt{good}}\right]+\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[x\notin\mathcal{X}_{\texttt{good}}\right].

To bound the first term in Eq. 111, note that if $x\in\mathcal{X}_{\texttt{good}}$, then $\pi^{\texttt{BoN}}_{N}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)\geq{}1-\delta/2$. Indeed, observe that $y\sim\pi^{\texttt{BoN}}_{N}(\cdot\mid{}x)\notin\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)$ if and only if $y_{1},\ldots,y_{N}\sim\pi_{\texttt{base}}(x)$ have $y_{i}\notin\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)$ for all $i$, which happens with probability $(1-\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x))^{N}\leq(1-1/N^{\star})^{N}\leq\delta/2$ since $x\in\mathcal{X}_{\texttt{good}}$. It follows that for any such $x$, we can lower bound (using the data processing inequality)

\displaystyle D^{2}_{\mathsf{H}}\left(\widehat{\pi}(\cdot\mid{}x),\pi^{\texttt{BoN}}_{N}(\cdot\mid{}x)\right) \displaystyle\geq\left(\sqrt{1-\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)}-\sqrt{1-\pi^{\texttt{BoN}}_{N}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)}\right)^{2} \displaystyle\gtrsim{}\delta\cdot\mathbb{I}\left\{\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)\leq{}1-\delta\right\}.
By Eqs. 108 and 113, it follows that
\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)\leq{}1-\delta,x\in\mathcal{X}_{\texttt{good}}\right]\lesssim\frac{\varepsilon_{\texttt{stat}}^{2}}{\delta}.
For the second term in Eq. 111, we bound

\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[x\notin\mathcal{X}_{\texttt{good}}\right] \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[N^{\star}<\frac{1}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)}\right] \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[\frac{1}{N^{\star}\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)}>1\right] \displaystyle\leq{}\frac{1}{N^{\star}}\En_{x\sim\mu}\left[\frac{1}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)}\right] \displaystyle\leq{}\frac{C_{\texttt{cov},\gamma}}{N^{\star}}
via Markov’s inequality and the definition of $C_{\texttt{cov},\gamma}$. Substituting both bounds into Eq. 111 completes the proof. ∎

Proof of Appendix D. The proof begins similarly to Section 4.1. By realizability of $\pi_{N_{\mu}}$, Section F.2 implies that the output of SFT-Sharpening satisfies, with probability at least $1-\rho$,

\displaystyle\En_{x\sim\mu}\left[D^{2}_{\mathsf{H}}\left(\widehat{\pi}(\cdot\mid{}x),\pi_{N_{\mu}}(\cdot\mid{}x)\right)\right]\leq\varepsilon_{\texttt{stat}}^{2}\vcentcolon={}\frac{2\log(\lvert\Pi\rvert/\rho)}{n}.

Condition on the event that this guarantee holds. We invoke the following lemma, proven in the sequel. Let $P$ be a distribution on a discrete space $\mathcal{Y}$. Let $\bm{y}^{\star}=\argmax_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}P(y)$ and let $P^{\star}:=\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}P(y)$. Let $y_{1},y_{2},\ldots\sim{}P$, and for any stopping time $\tau$, define
\displaystyle\widehat{y}_{\tau}\in\argmax\left\{P(y):y\in\left\{y_{1},\dots,y_{\tau}\right\}\right\}.
Next, for a parameter $\mu>0$, define the stopping time
\displaystyle N_{\mu}:=\inf\left\{k:\frac{1}{\max_{1\leq i\leq k}P(y_{i})}\leq k/\mu\right\}.
Then
\displaystyle\En[N_{\mu}]\leq\frac{\mu+(1/|\bm{y}^{\star}|)}{P^{\star}}.

In addition, for any stopping time $\tau\geq N_{\mu}$ (including $\tau=N_{\mu}$ itself), we have $\mathbb{P}[\widehat{y}_{\tau}\notin\bm{y}^{\star}]\leq e^{-\lvert\bm{y}^{\star}\rvert\mu}$. This lemma, with our choice of $\mu$, ensures that for all $x\in\mathcal{X}$,
\displaystyle\pi_{N_{\mu}}(\bm{y}^{\star}(x)\mid x)\geq 1-e^{-\mu}=1-\delta/2.
Following the reasoning in Eq. 113, this implies that
\displaystyle D^{2}_{\mathsf{H}}\left(\widehat{\pi}(\cdot\mid{}x),\pi_{N_{\mu}}(\cdot\mid{}x)\right)\gtrsim{}\delta\cdot\mathbb{I}\left\{\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\star}(x)\mid{}x)\leq{}1-\delta\right\},
so that
\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\star}(x)\mid{}x)\leq{}1-\delta\right]\lesssim\frac{\varepsilon_{\texttt{stat}}^{2}}{\delta}
as desired.
To bound the expected sample complexity, we observe that

\displaystyle\En[m]=n\cdot\En[N_{\mu}(x)]\overset{(i)}{\leq}\En\left[\frac{1+\mu}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\bm{y}^{\star}(x)\mid x)}\right]=(1+\mu)\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{C}_{\texttt{cov}},
where inequality $(i)$ invokes Appendix I once more. ∎
Proof of Appendix I. Define $N^{\star}:=\mu/P^{\star}$. To bound the tails of $N_{\mu}$, define
\displaystyle\tau=\inf\{k\mid{}k\geq N^{\star}\text{ and }\bm{y}^{\star}\cap\{y_{1},\dots,y_{k}\}\neq\varnothing\}.
It follows from the definition that $N_{\mu}\leq\tau$, since for any $k\geq{}N^{\star}$, if there exists $i\leq{}k$ such that $y_{i}\in\bm{y}^{\star}$, then
\displaystyle\frac{1}{P(y_{i})}=\frac{1}{P^{\star}}=\frac{N^{\star}}{\mu}\leq\frac{k}{\mu}.
Thus, for $k\geq N^{\star}$, we can bound
\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[N_{\mu}>k]\leq\mathbb{P}[\tau>k]=\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{Y}^{\star}\cap\{y_{1},\dots,y_{k}\}=\varnothing]\leq(1-|\bm{y}^{\star}|P^{\star})^{k},
and consequently

\displaystyle\En[N_{\mu}]\leq\En[\tau] \displaystyle\leq\En[\tau\mathbb{I}\{\tau\leq N^{\star}\}]+\En[\tau\mathbb{I}\{\tau>N^{\star}\}] \displaystyle\leq N^{\star}+\sum_{k>N^{\star}}(1-|\bm{y}^{\star}|P^{\star})^{k} \displaystyle\leq N^{\star}+\frac{1}{|\bm{y}^{\star}|P(y^{\star})}=\frac{\mu+1/|\bm{y}^{\star}|}{P(y^{\star})}.

To prove correctness, observe that $N_{\mu}\geq N^{\star}$, because for all $y\in\mathcal{Y}$, $\frac{1}{P(y)}\geq N^{\star}/\mu$. Hence, any stopping time $\tau\geq N_{\mu}$ also satisfies $\tau\geq N^{\star}$, and moreover has $\widehat{y}_{\tau}\in\bm{y}^{\star}$ whenever $\bm{y}^{\star}\cap\{y_{1},y_{2},\dots,y_{\tau}\}\neq\varnothing$. This fails to occur with probability no more than
\displaystyle\left(1-\frac{|\bm{y}^{\star}|}{P^{\star}}\right)^{N^{\star}}=\left(1-\frac{|\bm{y}^{\star}|}{P^{\star}}\right)^{\mu/P^{\star}}\leq e^{-|\bm{y}^{\star}|\mu}.

The following theorem is a generalization of Section 4.1 which allows for approximate maximizers in the sense of Section F.1. Let $\rho,\delta\in(0,1)$ be given, and suppose we set $N=N^{\star}\log(2\delta^{-1})$ for a parameter $N^{\star}\in\mathbb{N}$. Then for any $n\in\mathbb{N}$, SFT-Sharpening ensures that with probability at least $1-\rho$, for any $\gamma\in(0,1)$, the output model $\widehat{\pi}$ satisfies

\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)\leq{}1-2\delta\right]\lesssim{}\frac{1}{\delta}\cdot{}\frac{\log(\lvert\Pi\rvert\rho^{-1})}{n}+\frac{C_{\texttt{cov},\gamma}}{N^{\star}}.

In particular, given $(\epsilon,\delta,\gamma)$, by setting $n=C_{\ref{thm:bestofn}}\frac{\log\lvert\Pi\rvert}{\delta\epsilon}$ and $N^{\star}=C_{\ref{thm:bestofn}}\frac{C_{\texttt{cov},\gamma}}{\epsilon}$ for a sufficiently large absolute constant $C_{\ref{thm:bestofn}}>0$, we are guaranteed that

\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)\leq{}1-\delta\right]\leq\epsilon.
