sections.title: J.2.4 Application: linear softmax models
path: J.2 Proof of Section 4.2.2 and Section 4.2.2

paragraphs.text: In this section we apply Section 4.2.2 to the class of linear softmax models, proving Section 4.2.2. This demonstrates that Algorithm 1 can achieve an exponential improvement in sample complexity compared to SFT-Sharpening.

[Linear softmax model] Let $d\in\mathbb{N}$ be given, and let $\phi:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}$ be a feature map with $\lVert\phi(x,y)\rVert_{2}\leq 1$ for all $x,y$. Let $\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}:\mathcal{X}\to\Delta(\mathcal{Y})$ be the uniform model $\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}(y\mid x):=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}|}$, and let $B\geq 1$. We consider the linear softmax model class $\Pi_{\phi,B}:=\{\pi_{\theta}:\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\lVert\theta\rVert_{2}\leq B\}$ where $\pi_{\theta}:\mathcal{X}\to\Delta(\mathcal{Y})$ is defined by
Footnote: 15 15 We use the notation $\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}$ to highlight the fact that $\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}=\pi_{\theta}$ for $\theta=0$.
\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)\propto\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}(y\mid x)\exp(\langle\phi(x,y),\theta\rangle).

[Restatement of Section 4.2.2] Let $\epsilon,\delta,\gamma_{\mathsf{margin}},\rho\in(0,1)$ be given. Suppose that $\pi_{\texttt{base}}=\pi_{\theta^{\star}}\in\Pi_{\phi,B}$ for some $\theta^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with $\lVert\theta^{\star}\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{\gamma_{\mathsf{margin}}B}{3\log(2|\mathcal{Y}|/\delta)}$. Also, suppose that $\pi_{\texttt{base}}$ satisfies Section 4.2 with parameter $\gamma_{\mathsf{margin}}$. Then Algorithm 1 with base model $\pi_{\texttt{base}}$, reward function $r(x,y):=\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(x,y)$, regularization parameter $\beta:=\gamma_{\mathsf{margin}}/(2\log(2|\mathcal{Y}|/\delta))$, and optimism parameter $\alpha(T)\propto\frac{\beta}{B+\log(|\mathcal{Y}|)}\sqrt{\frac{d\log(BdT/(\epsilon\delta))+\log(T/\rho)}{dT\log(T)}}$ returns an $(\epsilon,\delta)$-sharpened model with probability at least $1-\rho$, and has sample complexity
m=\mathrm{poly}(\epsilon^{-1},\delta^{-1},\gamma_{\mathsf{margin}}^{-1},d,B,\log(|\mathcal{Y}|/\rho)).

Before proving the result, we unpack the conditions. Section J.2.4 requires the base model $\pi_{\texttt{base}}$ to lie in the model class and also satisfy the margin condition (Section 4.2). For any constant $\epsilon,\delta>0$, the sharpening algorithm then succeeds with sample complexity $\mathrm{poly}(d,\gamma_{\mathsf{margin}}^{-1},B,\log(|\mathcal{Y}|))$. These conditions are non-vacuous; in fact, there are fairly natural examples for which non-exploratory algorithm such as SFT-Sharpening require sample complexity $\exp(\Omega(d))$, whereas all of the above parameters are $\mathrm{poly}(d)$. The following is one such example.

[Separation between RLHF-Sharpening and SFT-Sharpening ] Set $\mathcal{X}=\{x\}$ and let $\mathcal{Y}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}$ be a $1/4$-packing of the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ of cardinality $\exp(\Theta(d))$. Define $\phi:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}$ by $\phi(x,y):=y$, and let $B=Cd\log d$ for an absolute constant $C>0$. Fix any $y^{\star}\in\mathcal{Y}$ and define $\pi_{\texttt{base}}:=\pi_{\theta^{\star}}\in\Pi_{\phi,B}$ by $\theta^{\star}:=y^{\star}$. Then for any $y\neq y^{\star}$, we have $\langle y,y^{\star}\rangle\leq 1-\Omega(1)$, so
\frac{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y^{\star}\mid x)}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid x)}=\exp(\langle y^{\star}-y,y^{\star}\rangle)=\exp(\Omega(1))=1+\Omega(1).

Thus, $\pi_{\texttt{base}}$ satisfies Section 4.2 with $\gamma_{\mathsf{margin}}=\Omega(1)$. Moreover, $\lVert\theta^{\star}\rVert_{2}=1\leq\frac{\gamma_{\mathsf{margin}}B}{3\log(2|\mathcal{Y}|/\delta)}$ for any $\delta=1/\mathrm{poly}(d)$, so long as $C$ is a sufficiently large constant. It follows from Section 4.2.2 that Algorithm 1 computes an $(\epsilon,\delta)$-sharpened model with sample complexity $\mathrm{poly}(\epsilon^{-1},\delta^{-1},d)$. However, since $\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y^{\star}\mid x)\leq\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid x)\cdot\exp(2)$ for all $y\in\mathcal{Y}$, it is clear that
C_{\texttt{cov}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\bm{y}^{\star}(x)\mid x)}\right]=\frac{1}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y^{\star}\mid x)}=\Omega(|\mathcal{Y}|)=\exp(\Omega(d)).

Thus, the sample complexity guarantee for SFT-Sharpening in Section 4.1 will incur exponential dependence on $d$ in the sample complexity. It is straightforward to check that this dependence is real for SFT-Sharpening, and not just an artifact of the analysis, since the model that SFT-Sharpening is trying to learn (via MLE) will itself not be sharp in this example, unless $\exp(\Omega(d))$ samples are drawn per prompt.
We now proceed to the proof of Section J.2.4, which requires the following bounds on the covering number and the Sequential Extrapolation Coefficient of $\Pi_{\phi,B}$.
Let $\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}}>0$. Then $\Pi_{\phi,B}$ has an $\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}}$-net of size $(6B/\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}})^{d}$.

Proof of Section J.2.4. By a standard packing argument, there is a set $\{\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{N}\}$ of size $(6B/\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}})^{d}$ such that for every $\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with $\lVert\theta\rVert_{2}\leq B$ there is some $i\in[N]$ with $\lVert\theta_{i}-\theta\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}}/2$. Now for any $x\in\mathcal{X}$ and $y\in\mathcal{Y}$,

\displaystyle\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\theta_{i}}(y\mid x)} \displaystyle=\log\frac{\exp(\langle\phi(x,y),\theta\rangle)}{\exp(\langle\phi(x,y),\theta_{i}\rangle)}+\log\frac{\E_{(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\sim\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}}\exp(\langle\phi(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}),\theta_{i}\rangle)}{\E_{(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\sim\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}}\exp(\langle\phi(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}),\theta\rangle)} \displaystyle=\langle\phi(x,y),\theta-\theta_{i}\rangle+\log\frac{\E_{(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\sim\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}}\left[\exp(\langle\phi(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}),\theta\rangle)\exp(\langle\phi(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}),\theta_{i}-\theta\rangle)\right]}{\E_{(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\sim\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}}\exp(\langle\phi(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}),\theta\rangle)}.

The first term is bounded by $\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}}/2$ in magnitude. In the second term, we have $\exp(\langle\phi(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}),\theta_{i}-\theta\rangle)\in[\exp(-\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}}/2),\exp(\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}}/2)]$, so the ratio of expectations lies in $[\exp(-\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}}/2),\exp(\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}}/2)]$ as well, and so the log-ratio lies in $[-\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}}/2,\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}}/2]$. In all, we get $\left|\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y|x)}{\pi_{\theta_{i}}(y\mid x)}\right|\leq\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}}$. Thus, $\{\pi_{\theta_{1}},\dots,\pi_{\theta_{N}}\}$ is an $\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}}$-net for $\Pi$. ∎

Let $r:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to[-R_{\mathsf{max}},R_{\mathsf{max}}]$ be a reward function and let $T\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\beta>0$. If $\lambda\geq 4\beta^{2}B^{2}+R_{\mathsf{max}}^{2}$ then for any $\pi^{\star}\in\Pi_{\phi,B}$,
\mathsf{SEC}(\Pi_{\phi,B},r,T,\beta,\lambda;\pi^{\star})\lesssim d\log(T+1).
Proof of Section J.2.4. Fix $\pi^{(1)},\dots,\pi^{(T)}\in\Pi_{\phi,B}.$ By definition, there are some $\theta^{(1)},\dots,\theta^{(T)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with $\lVert\theta^{(t)}\rVert_{2}\leq B$ and
\pi^{(t)}(y\mid x)\propto\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}(y\mid x)\exp(\langle\phi(x,y),\theta^{(t)}\rangle)

for all $t\in[T]$ and $(x,y)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}$. Similarly, there is some $\theta^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with $\lVert\theta^{\star}\rVert_{2}\leq B$ and $\pi^{\star}(y\mid x)\propto\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}(y\mid x)\exp(\langle\phi(x,y),\theta^{\star}\rangle)$.

Define $\widetilde{\phi}:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}^{d+1}$ by $\widetilde{\phi}(x,y):=[\phi(x,y),\frac{r(x,y)}{R_{\mathsf{max}}}]$ and define $\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)}:=[\beta(\theta^{(t)}-\theta^{\star}),-R_{\mathsf{max}}]$. Then for any $t\in[T]$ we have

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}^{(t)}\left[\beta\log\frac{\pi^{(t)}(y\mid x)}{\pi^{\star}(y\mid x)}-r(x,y)-\beta\log\frac{\pi^{(t)}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}{\pi^{\star}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}+r(x,y^{\prime})\right]^{2}}{\lambda\lor\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\mathbb{E}^{(i)}\left[\left(\beta\log\frac{\pi^{(t)}(y\mid x)}{\pi^{\star}(y\mid x)}-r(x,y)-\beta\log\frac{\pi^{(t)}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}{\pi^{\star}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}+r(x,y^{\prime})\right)^{2}\right]} \displaystyle=\frac{\mathbb{E}^{(t)}\left[\langle\widetilde{\phi}(x,y)-\widetilde{\phi}(x,y^{\prime}),\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)}\rangle\right]^{2}}{\lambda\lor\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\mathbb{E}^{(i)}\left[\left(\langle\widetilde{\phi}(x,y)-\widetilde{\phi}(x,y^{\prime}),\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)}\rangle\right)^{2}\right]} \displaystyle\leq\frac{(\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)})^{\top}\Sigma^{(t)}\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)}}{\lambda\lor\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}(\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)})^{\top}\Sigma^{(i)}\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)}}

where for each $i\in[T]$ we have defined $\Sigma^{(i)}:=\mathbb{E}^{(i)}\left[(\widetilde{\phi}(x,y)-\widetilde{\phi}(x,y^{\prime}))(\widetilde{\phi}(x,y)-\widetilde{\phi}(x,y^{\prime}))^{\top}\right]$. Observe that $\lVert\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)}\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq 4\beta^{2}B^{2}+R_{\mathsf{max}}^{2}\leq\lambda$ by assumption on $\lambda$. Therefore,

\displaystyle\frac{(\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)})^{\top}\Sigma^{(t)}\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)}}{\lambda\lor\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}(\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)})^{\top}\Sigma^{(i)}\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)}} \displaystyle\lesssim\frac{(\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)})^{\top}\Sigma^{(t)}\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)}}{\lambda+\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}(\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)})^{\top}\Sigma^{(i)}\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)}} \displaystyle\leq\frac{(\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)})^{\top}\Sigma^{(t)}\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)}}{(\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)})^{\top}\left(I_{d}+\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\Sigma^{(i)}\right)\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)}} \displaystyle\leq\lambda_{\max}\left(\left(I_{d}+\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\Sigma^{(i)}\right)^{-1/2}\Sigma^{(t)}\left(I_{d}+\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\Sigma^{(i)}\right)^{-1/2}\right) \displaystyle\leq\Tr\left(\left(I_{d}+\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\Sigma^{(i)}\right)^{-1/2}\Sigma^{(t)}\left(I_{d}+\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\Sigma^{(i)}\right)^{-1/2}\right) \displaystyle=\Tr\left(\left(I_{d}+\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\Sigma^{(i)}\right)^{-1}\Sigma^{(t)}\right).
Observe that $\Tr(\Sigma^{(t)})\leq\max_{x,y}\lVert\widetilde{\phi}(x,y)\rVert_{2}^{2}\lesssim 1$. Hence by Section F.2, we have

\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{\mathbb{E}^{(t)}\left[\beta\log\frac{\pi^{(t)}(y\mid x)}{\pi^{\star}(y\mid x)}-r(x,y)-\beta\log\frac{\pi^{(t)}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}{\pi^{\star}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}+r(x,y^{\prime})\right]^{2}}{\lambda\lor\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\mathbb{E}^{(i)}\left[\left(\beta\log\frac{\pi^{(t)}(y\mid x)}{\pi^{\star}(y\mid x)}-r(x,y)-\beta\log\frac{\pi^{(t)}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}{\pi^{\star}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}+r(x,y^{\prime})\right)^{2}\right]} \displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{t=1}^{T}\Tr\left(\left(I_{d}+\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\Sigma^{(i)}\right)^{-1}\Sigma^{(t)}\right) \displaystyle\lesssim d\log(T+1).
Since $\pi^{(1)},\dots,\pi^{(T)}\in\Pi$ were arbitrary, this completes the proof. ∎
The proof is now immediate from Section J.2.3 and the above lemmas.

Proof of Section J.2.4. By the assumption on $\theta^{\star}$ and choice of $\beta$, the model $\pi^{\star}_{\beta}$ defined by $\pi^{\star}_{\beta}(y\mid x)\propto\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid x)^{1+\beta^{-1}}$ satisfies $\pi^{\star}_{\beta}=\pi_{(1+\beta^{-1})\theta^{\star}}\in\Pi_{\phi,B}$. By Section J.2.4, we have $\mathcal{N}(\Pi_{\phi,B},\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}})\leq(6B/\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}})^{d}$. Take $R_{\mathsf{max}}:=\sqrt{4\beta^{2}B^{2}+(2B+\log|\mathcal{Y}|)^{2}}$. We know that $r(x,y):=\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid x)$ satisfies $|r(x,y)|\leq 2B+\log|\mathcal{Y}|$ for all $x,y$. By Section J.2.4, we therefore get that $\mathsf{SEC}(\Pi_{\phi,B},r,T,\beta,R_{\mathsf{max}}^{2};\pi_{\texttt{base}})\lesssim d\log(T+1)$. Substituting these bounds into Section J.2.3 yields the claimed result. ∎

In this section we apply Section 4.2.2 to the class of linear softmax models, proving Section 4.2.2. This demonstrates that Algorithm 1 can achieve an exponential improvement in sample complexity compared to SFT-Sharpening.

[Linear softmax model] Let $d\in\mathbb{N}$ be given, and let $\phi:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}$ be a feature map with $\lVert\phi(x,y)\rVert_{2}\leq 1$ for all $x,y$. Let $\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}:\mathcal{X}\to\Delta(\mathcal{Y})$ be the uniform model $\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}(y\mid x):=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}|}$, and let $B\geq 1$. We consider the linear softmax model class $\Pi_{\phi,B}:=\{\pi_{\theta}:\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\lVert\theta\rVert_{2}\leq B\}$ where $\pi_{\theta}:\mathcal{X}\to\Delta(\mathcal{Y})$ is defined by

Footnote: 15 15 We use the notation $\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}$ to highlight the fact that $\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}=\pi_{\theta}$ for $\theta=0$.

\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)\propto\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}(y\mid x)\exp(\langle\phi(x,y),\theta\rangle).

[Restatement of Section 4.2.2] Let $\epsilon,\delta,\gamma_{\mathsf{margin}},\rho\in(0,1)$ be given. Suppose that $\pi_{\texttt{base}}=\pi_{\theta^{\star}}\in\Pi_{\phi,B}$ for some $\theta^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with $\lVert\theta^{\star}\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{\gamma_{\mathsf{margin}}B}{3\log(2|\mathcal{Y}|/\delta)}$. Also, suppose that $\pi_{\texttt{base}}$ satisfies Section 4.2 with parameter $\gamma_{\mathsf{margin}}$. Then Algorithm 1 with base model $\pi_{\texttt{base}}$, reward function $r(x,y):=\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(x,y)$, regularization parameter $\beta:=\gamma_{\mathsf{margin}}/(2\log(2|\mathcal{Y}|/\delta))$, and optimism parameter $\alpha(T)\propto\frac{\beta}{B+\log(|\mathcal{Y}|)}\sqrt{\frac{d\log(BdT/(\epsilon\delta))+\log(T/\rho)}{dT\log(T)}}$ returns an $(\epsilon,\delta)$-sharpened model with probability at least $1-\rho$, and has sample complexity

m=\mathrm{poly}(\epsilon^{-1},\delta^{-1},\gamma_{\mathsf{margin}}^{-1},d,B,\log(|\mathcal{Y}|/\rho)).

Before proving the result, we unpack the conditions. Section J.2.4 requires the base model $\pi_{\texttt{base}}$ to lie in the model class and also satisfy the margin condition (Section 4.2). For any constant $\epsilon,\delta>0$, the sharpening algorithm then succeeds with sample complexity $\mathrm{poly}(d,\gamma_{\mathsf{margin}}^{-1},B,\log(|\mathcal{Y}|))$. These conditions are non-vacuous; in fact, there are fairly natural examples for which non-exploratory algorithm such as SFT-Sharpening require sample complexity $\exp(\Omega(d))$, whereas all of the above parameters are $\mathrm{poly}(d)$. The following is one such example.

C_{\texttt{cov}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\bm{y}^{\star}(x)\mid x)}\right]=\frac{1}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y^{\star}\mid x)}=\Omega(|\mathcal{Y}|)=\exp(\Omega(d)).

We now proceed to the proof of Section J.2.4, which requires the following bounds on the covering number and the Sequential Extrapolation Coefficient of $\Pi_{\phi,B}$.

Let $\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}}>0$. Then $\Pi_{\phi,B}$ has an $\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}}$-net of size $(6B/\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}})^{d}$.

By a standard packing argument, there is a set $\{\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{N}\}$ of size $(6B/\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}})^{d}$ such that for every $\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with $\lVert\theta\rVert_{2}\leq B$ there is some $i\in[N]$ with $\lVert\theta_{i}-\theta\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}}/2$. Now for any $x\in\mathcal{X}$ and $y\in\mathcal{Y}$,

\displaystyle\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\theta_{i}}(y\mid x)} \displaystyle=\log\frac{\exp(\langle\phi(x,y),\theta\rangle)}{\exp(\langle\phi(x,y),\theta_{i}\rangle)}+\log\frac{\E_{(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\sim\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}}\exp(\langle\phi(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}),\theta_{i}\rangle)}{\E_{(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\sim\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}}\exp(\langle\phi(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}),\theta\rangle)} \displaystyle=\langle\phi(x,y),\theta-\theta_{i}\rangle+\log\frac{\E_{(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\sim\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}}\left[\exp(\langle\phi(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}),\theta\rangle)\exp(\langle\phi(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}),\theta_{i}-\theta\rangle)\right]}{\E_{(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\sim\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}}\exp(\langle\phi(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}),\theta\rangle)}.

Let $r:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to[-R_{\mathsf{max}},R_{\mathsf{max}}]$ be a reward function and let $T\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\beta>0$. If $\lambda\geq 4\beta^{2}B^{2}+R_{\mathsf{max}}^{2}$ then for any $\pi^{\star}\in\Pi_{\phi,B}$,

\mathsf{SEC}(\Pi_{\phi,B},r,T,\beta,\lambda;\pi^{\star})\lesssim d\log(T+1).

Proof of Section J.2.4. Fix $\pi^{(1)},\dots,\pi^{(T)}\in\Pi_{\phi,B}.$ By definition, there are some $\theta^{(1)},\dots,\theta^{(T)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with $\lVert\theta^{(t)}\rVert_{2}\leq B$ and

\pi^{(t)}(y\mid x)\propto\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}(y\mid x)\exp(\langle\phi(x,y),\theta^{(t)}\rangle)

for all $t\in[T]$ and $(x,y)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}$. Similarly, there is some $\theta^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with $\lVert\theta^{\star}\rVert_{2}\leq B$ and $\pi^{\star}(y\mid x)\propto\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}(y\mid x)\exp(\langle\phi(x,y),\theta^{\star}\rangle)$.

Define $\widetilde{\phi}:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}^{d+1}$ by $\widetilde{\phi}(x,y):=[\phi(x,y),\frac{r(x,y)}{R_{\mathsf{max}}}]$ and define $\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)}:=[\beta(\theta^{(t)}-\theta^{\star}),-R_{\mathsf{max}}]$. Then for any $t\in[T]$ we have

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}^{(t)}\left[\beta\log\frac{\pi^{(t)}(y\mid x)}{\pi^{\star}(y\mid x)}-r(x,y)-\beta\log\frac{\pi^{(t)}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}{\pi^{\star}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}+r(x,y^{\prime})\right]^{2}}{\lambda\lor\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\mathbb{E}^{(i)}\left[\left(\beta\log\frac{\pi^{(t)}(y\mid x)}{\pi^{\star}(y\mid x)}-r(x,y)-\beta\log\frac{\pi^{(t)}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}{\pi^{\star}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}+r(x,y^{\prime})\right)^{2}\right]} \displaystyle=\frac{\mathbb{E}^{(t)}\left[\langle\widetilde{\phi}(x,y)-\widetilde{\phi}(x,y^{\prime}),\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)}\rangle\right]^{2}}{\lambda\lor\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\mathbb{E}^{(i)}\left[\left(\langle\widetilde{\phi}(x,y)-\widetilde{\phi}(x,y^{\prime}),\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)}\rangle\right)^{2}\right]} \displaystyle\leq\frac{(\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)})^{\top}\Sigma^{(t)}\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)}}{\lambda\lor\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}(\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)})^{\top}\Sigma^{(i)}\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)}}

where for each $i\in[T]$ we have defined $\Sigma^{(i)}:=\mathbb{E}^{(i)}\left[(\widetilde{\phi}(x,y)-\widetilde{\phi}(x,y^{\prime}))(\widetilde{\phi}(x,y)-\widetilde{\phi}(x,y^{\prime}))^{\top}\right]$. Observe that $\lVert\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)}\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq 4\beta^{2}B^{2}+R_{\mathsf{max}}^{2}\leq\lambda$ by assumption on $\lambda$. Therefore,

\displaystyle\frac{(\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)})^{\top}\Sigma^{(t)}\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)}}{\lambda\lor\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}(\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)})^{\top}\Sigma^{(i)}\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)}} \displaystyle\lesssim\frac{(\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)})^{\top}\Sigma^{(t)}\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)}}{\lambda+\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}(\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)})^{\top}\Sigma^{(i)}\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)}} \displaystyle\leq\frac{(\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)})^{\top}\Sigma^{(t)}\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)}}{(\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)})^{\top}\left(I_{d}+\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\Sigma^{(i)}\right)\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)}} \displaystyle\leq\lambda_{\max}\left(\left(I_{d}+\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\Sigma^{(i)}\right)^{-1/2}\Sigma^{(t)}\left(I_{d}+\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\Sigma^{(i)}\right)^{-1/2}\right) \displaystyle\leq\Tr\left(\left(I_{d}+\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\Sigma^{(i)}\right)^{-1/2}\Sigma^{(t)}\left(I_{d}+\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\Sigma^{(i)}\right)^{-1/2}\right) \displaystyle=\Tr\left(\left(I_{d}+\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\Sigma^{(i)}\right)^{-1}\Sigma^{(t)}\right).

Observe that $\Tr(\Sigma^{(t)})\leq\max_{x,y}\lVert\widetilde{\phi}(x,y)\rVert_{2}^{2}\lesssim 1$. Hence by Section F.2, we have

\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{\mathbb{E}^{(t)}\left[\beta\log\frac{\pi^{(t)}(y\mid x)}{\pi^{\star}(y\mid x)}-r(x,y)-\beta\log\frac{\pi^{(t)}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}{\pi^{\star}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}+r(x,y^{\prime})\right]^{2}}{\lambda\lor\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\mathbb{E}^{(i)}\left[\left(\beta\log\frac{\pi^{(t)}(y\mid x)}{\pi^{\star}(y\mid x)}-r(x,y)-\beta\log\frac{\pi^{(t)}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}{\pi^{\star}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}+r(x,y^{\prime})\right)^{2}\right]} \displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{t=1}^{T}\Tr\left(\left(I_{d}+\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\Sigma^{(i)}\right)^{-1}\Sigma^{(t)}\right) \displaystyle\lesssim d\log(T+1).

Since $\pi^{(1)},\dots,\pi^{(T)}\in\Pi$ were arbitrary, this completes the proof. ∎

The proof is now immediate from Section J.2.3 and the above lemmas.

Proof of Section J.2.4. By the assumption on $\theta^{\star}$ and choice of $\beta$, the model $\pi^{\star}_{\beta}$ defined by $\pi^{\star}_{\beta}(y\mid x)\propto\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid x)^{1+\beta^{-1}}$ satisfies $\pi^{\star}_{\beta}=\pi_{(1+\beta^{-1})\theta^{\star}}\in\Pi_{\phi,B}$. By Section J.2.4, we have $\mathcal{N}(\Pi_{\phi,B},\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}})\leq(6B/\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}})^{d}$. Take $R_{\mathsf{max}}:=\sqrt{4\beta^{2}B^{2}+(2B+\log|\mathcal{Y}|)^{2}}$. We know that $r(x,y):=\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid x)$ satisfies $|r(x,y)|\leq 2B+\log|\mathcal{Y}|$ for all $x,y$. By Section J.2.4, we therefore get that $\mathsf{SEC}(\Pi_{\phi,B},r,T,\beta,R_{\mathsf{max}}^{2};\pi_{\texttt{base}})\lesssim d\log(T+1)$.
